lessons.title: Compare hash collisions with Snowflake code length
lessons.summary: Uniform truncated hashes still need atomic code collision detection and retries.
lessons.body:
## Deep dive 1: Generating short codes

This is the heart of the problem. You need billions of unique, short, ideally unguessable codes, generated by many servers without a global lock.

### Option A: Hash the long URL

Hash the URL with SHA-256 and map it approximately uniformly into the base62 code space. The collision arithmetic below assumes uniform codes; naively taking leading digits of a variable-width integer encoding can introduce bias.

- **Pro**: stateless; any server can compute it.
- **Con: collisions.** Truncating to 7 characters leaves a 3.5-trillion space. By the [birthday problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birthday_problem), the collision probability is about 39% by 1.9 million links and about 50% by 2.2 million (worked out below). With hundreds of billions of links you will collide constantly, so every write needs an atomic insert-if-absent and a retry on conflict (for example, appending a counter and rehashing).
- **Con: same URL, same code.** Two users shortening the same URL get the same link, which breaks per-owner analytics and expiry. You can salt with the user ID, but then you lose the dedup that was the main appeal.

Where does "about 1.9 million" come from? The birthday problem asks how many random values you can draw from a space before two of them are likely to match. The answer grows with the *square root* of the space, which is far smaller than the space itself:

```formula
n_50 ≈ 1.18√(N)
√(N) = √(3.5 × 10^12) ≈ 1.9 × 10^6
n_50 ≈ 1.18 × 1.9 × 10^6 ≈ 2.2 × 10^6
where
N: the number of possible codes, here 62^7 ≈ 3.5 × 10^12 (3.5 trillion)
√: square root, the number that multiplied by itself gives the value inside
n_50: how many random codes you can issue before there is a 50% chance that at least two are the same
1.18: the constant √(2 × ln 2) ≈ 1.1774 from the standard birthday-problem approximation (ln is the natural logarithm)
10^6, 10^12: a million and a trillion
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: in a space of 3.5 trillion codes, a repeat becomes a coin flip after only about 2 million random codes.
```

At about 1.9 million uniformly random codes the chance of at least one collision is already about 39%. The approximation assumes codes are spread uniformly at random, which a good hash gives. A shortener issuing billions of links is a thousand times past this point, so collisions are routine, not rare.

### Option C: Snowflake-style IDs

[Snowflake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snowflake_ID), from Twitter, packs a 64-bit ID as:

```
| 1 | 41 bits ms | 10 bits  | 12 bits |
|   | timestamp  | machine  | seq     |
```

Each field's size in bits fixes how many values it can hold:

```formula
seq = 2^12 = 4,096
time = 2^41 ms ≈ 69.7 years
where
seq: distinct sequence numbers one worker can issue in one millisecond
time: how long the 41-bit millisecond timestamp lasts before it wraps round
2^12, 2^41: 12 or 41 copies of 2 multiplied together; a field of b bits holds 2^b different values
ms: millisecond, a thousandth of a second
years: calendar years
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: 12 bits of sequence allow 4,096 IDs per worker per millisecond, and 41 bits of milliseconds last about 70 years from the chosen start date.
```

Each worker has 4,096 sequence values per millisecond. Generation avoids per-ID coordination, but worker IDs must be assigned uniquely and restart/clock behavior must prevent reuse.

- **Pro**: fully decentralised, roughly time-ordered.
- **Con: length.** The original Snowflake layout has 63 usable bits. An ID above a quintillion (a 1 followed by 18 zeros) takes **11 base62 characters**, not 7 (see below). For a *short*ener, that's a real cost.
- **Con: clocks.** If a machine's clock goes backwards (NTP correction), it can reissue IDs unless the generator refuses to run until the clock catches up.

Why can it need 11 characters? Compare an assumed ID above a quintillion with the code capacities:

```formula
62^10 ≈ 8.4 × 10^17
62^11 ≈ 5.2 × 10^19
where
62^10, 62^11: the number of values that 10 and 11 base62 characters can represent
10^17, 10^19: 1 followed by 17 or 19 zeros
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: ten characters cover values up to about 8 × 10^17, but a Snowflake ID above a quintillion needs eleven.
```

## Key takeaways

- Uniform truncated hashes still need atomic code collision detection and retries.
- The birthday threshold grows with the square root of the code space.
- Snowflake avoids per-ID coordination but needs unique workers, safe clocks and longer codes.

## Further reading

- [Twitter: original Snowflake worker implementation](https://github.com/twitter-archive/snowflake/blob/snowflake-2010/src/main/scala/com/twitter/service/snowflake/IdWorker.scala)
- [Birthday problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birthday_problem)

questions.prompt: A colleague proposes generating codes by taking the first 7 base62 characters of `SHA-256(longUrl)`. The service will hold hundreds of billions of links. What is the main problem?

options.text: SHA-256 is too slow to compute at 3,000 writes per second.
options.explanation: Wrong. No hardware benchmark is supplied; the demonstrated problem is namespace collisions, not an established hashing bottleneck.

options.text: Hash-based codes can't be stored in a key-value store.
options.explanation: Wrong. A hash-derived code is just a string key; any KV store handles it. The issue is uniqueness, not storage.

options.text: Truncated hashes collide frequently at this scale, so every write needs an existence check and retry, and identical URLs from different users map to the same code.
options.explanation: Correct. With a 3.5-trillion space, the birthday bound puts a 50% chance of at least one collision at ~2.2 million links. At hundreds of billions, a meaningful fraction of new inserts will collide, and dedup by URL breaks per-user ownership, expiry and analytics.

options.text: Hashes are reversible, so attackers can recover the long URL from the code.
options.explanation: Wrong. Cryptographic hashes are designed to make finding an input for a specified output computationally difficult. A truncated code loses information and cannot uniquely identify its original URL; finding a matching guessed input is a different task and a shorter output can make matching easier. Predictable input URLs can still be guessed and hashed, and a densely occupied short namespace can be probed.

questions.workedExample:
The arithmetic assumes uniformly distributed codes. Taking leading digits of a variable-width integer encoding can introduce bias; use an approximately uniform mapping before relying on this model. Apply the birthday problem: when you draw random values from a space, repeats turn up far sooner than intuition suggests, after roughly the *square root* of the space size.

```formula
n_50 ≈ 1.18√(N)
N = 62^7 ≈ 3.5 × 10^12
√(N) ≈ 1.88 × 10^6
n_50 ≈ 2.2 × 10^6
where
N: the number of possible 7-character base62 codes
√: square root, the number that multiplied by itself gives the value inside
n_50: how many random codes you can issue before a 50% chance that two are the same
1.18: the constant √(2 × ln 2) from the birthday approximation (ln is the natural logarithm)
10^6, 10^12: a million and a trillion
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: in a 3.5-trillion space, a repeat becomes a coin flip after about 2.2 million random codes.
```

Once the space is partly full, each new random code collides with probability equal to the fraction already used:

```formula
p = stored / N
p = (350 × 10^9) / (3.5 × 10^12) = 0.1
where
p: the chance a fresh random code is already taken
stored: links already held, here 350 billion
N: total possible codes, 3.5 trillion
In words: with a tenth of the codes used, one new code in ten collides.
```

So one write in ten collides and needs a retry, each requiring an atomic conditional insert, not a racy read-before-write. Add the dedup problem (same URL → same code for every user) and a counter-based scheme is much simpler.

lessons.title: Allocate counter ranges and shuffle codes
lessons.summary: Allocate non-overlapping ranges durably and never reuse them after crashes.
lessons.body:
The previous unit compared truncated hashes and Snowflake IDs. This unit develops the counter alternative: keep codes short and collision-free while moving coordination out of the per-link hot path.

### Option B: A counter, base62-encoded

Give each link the next integer and base62-encode it. Base62 is ordinary place-value notation, like decimal, but each position is worth 62 times the one to its right instead of 10 times. With the alphabet ordered `0–9`, `a–z`, `A–Z`:

```formula
n = 62d_1 + d_0
125 = 2 × 62 + 1 → "21"
62^7 − 1 → "ZZZZZZZ"
where
n: the counter value being encoded
d_0: the value of the rightmost character, from 0 to 61 (0–9 are 0–9, a–z are 10–35, A–Z are 36–61)
d_1: the value of the next character to the left, worth 62 each
62^7 − 1: the largest number that fits in 7 base62 characters, about 3.5 trillion
→: "is written as"
In words: 125 is two 62s plus one, so it is written "21"; the largest 7-character code, "ZZZZZZZ", stands for 62^7 − 1.
```

Longer codes just add positions worth 62², 62³ and so on.

- **Pro**: no collisions, ever. Codes are as short as possible.
- **Con**: a single global counter is a bottleneck and single point of failure.
- **Fix: range allocation.** A coordination service (a small database table, ZooKeeper or etcd) hands each write server a *block* of, say, 1 million IDs. The server allocates from its block in memory and only goes back for a new block when it runs out. At 3,000 writes/s, the coordinator is contacted once every few minutes (worked out below). If a server crashes, the rest of its block is simply wasted. With 3.5 trillion codes, wasting millions is irrelevant.
- **Con: guessable.** Sequential codes let anyone enumerate links (`aaaaaab`, `aaaaaac`...). Fix this by passing the counter through a reversible permutation before encoding: for example, multiply by a large constant that shares no factor with 62^7 (so not a multiple of 2 or 31) modulo 62^7, or use a small Feistel network keyed with a secret. It stays collision-free (it's a bijection) but looks random. The multiplication trick only hides the pattern from casual eyes (decoded codes from known consecutive counters reveal the multiplier through their modular difference); a vetted keyed permutation can hide sequence relationships, but a custom small Feistel construction is not established as secure here.

How often the coordinator is contacted is the block size divided by the write rate:

```formula
t = block / writes
t = 1,000,000 / (3,000/s) ≈ 333 s
where
t: the time between requests for a new block, in seconds (s)
block: IDs handed out per request, here 1 million
writes: links created per second across the fleet, here the 3,000/s peak
/s: per second
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: a million-ID block lasts about five and a half minutes at peak, so the coordinator sees about eleven block requests an hour across the fleet at steady peak, excluding the initial allocations and wasted ranges.
```

The multiply-and-wrap bijective shuffle from the "guessable" bullet looks like this:

```formula
m = (an) mod 62^7
where
n: the counter value, from 0 up to 62^7 − 1
a: a large constant that shares no factor with 62^7, so it is not a multiple of 2 or 31 (62 = 2 × 31)
mod: modulo, the remainder after division; it wraps the product back into the range 0 to 62^7 − 1
m: the shuffled value, which is then base62-encoded into the 7-character code
In words: multiply the counter by a fixed constant and keep the remainder; because the constant shares no factor with the size of the code space, no two counter values end up with the same code.
```

### Option D: Pre-generated key service

A key generation service pre-computes random 7-character codes, stores them in an "unused" table, and hands batches to write servers. It's essentially Option B with random rather than sequential codes. It works, but you have to store and manage billions of unused keys.

> [!tip] Recommended answer
> Range-allocated counters with a bijective shuffle, base62-encoded to 7 characters. Collision-free and short when ranges are never reused; the bijective shuffle is not an access-control mechanism, and the coordinator is touched only once per million links.

## Key takeaways

- Allocate non-overlapping ranges durably and never reuse them after crashes.
- A coprime multiply-and-wrap mapping preserves uniqueness.
- A bijection is not authorisation or proof of cryptographic security.

## Further reading

- [Python: numeric operations and divmod](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#divmod)
- [DynamoDB: conditional writes](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/Expressions.ConditionExpressions.html)

questions.prompt: You use range allocation: a coordinator hands each write server a block of **1,000,000** IDs. Peak write rate is **3,000 links/s** across 10 servers. Roughly how often does the coordinator receive a block request, and what happens if a server crashes mid-block?

options.text: About 3,000 times per second; the crash corrupts the counter.
options.explanation: Wrong. That would be the rate with no batching at all. With 1M-ID blocks the coordinator is consulted once per million IDs, and a crash cannot corrupt a counter that has already moved past the block.

options.text: About once every 5–6 minutes in total; the unused IDs in the crashed server's block are simply skipped.
options.explanation: Correct. 1M / 3,000 ≈ 333 s between block requests overall. Unused IDs are wasted, but with 3.5 trillion codes, losing a million per crash is negligible, and no ID is ever issued twice.

options.text: About once per day; the crashed block is reassigned to another server.
options.explanation: Wrong on both counts. At 3,000/s you consume 1M IDs in ~5.5 minutes, not a day. Reassigning a partially used block is dangerous because you don't know which IDs were already issued.

options.text: Never; each server generates IDs from its own clock.
options.explanation: Wrong. That describes Snowflake-style generation, which needs no coordinator, not range allocation.

questions.workedExample:
The coordinator is asked once per block, so the time between requests is the block size divided by the write rate.

```formula
t = block / writes
t = 1,000,000 / (3,000/s) ≈ 333 s
t_server = 1,000,000 / (300/s) ≈ 3,333 s
where
t: time between block requests across the whole fleet, in seconds (s)
block: IDs per block, 1 million
writes: global peak write rate, 3,000 links per second
t_server: time between requests from one server, which sees a tenth of the writes (300/s)
/s: per second
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: the fleet asks for a block about every 5.5 minutes, and each server about once an hour.
```

That's why the coordinator isn't a bottleneck.

On a crash, the coordinator has already advanced past the block, so the remaining IDs are never handed out again. Waste per crash is at most 1 million IDs; even 1,000 crashes waste 1 billion, under 0.03% of the 3.5 trillion 7-character codes.

questions.prompt: A usability review flags that your counter-based codes are sequential: `aZ3kQ9x` is followed by `aZ3kQ9y`, revealing sequential allocation. Private-link access control is handled separately. Which algebraic approach keeps codes collision-free and 7 characters long?

options.text: Switch to random 7-character codes and retry on collision.
options.explanation: Partly works but reintroduces the collision problem: at 10% fill, one write in ten collides and needs a atomic insert-if-absent retry. You've traded a security problem for a correctness and latency one.

options.text: Use Snowflake IDs instead.
options.explanation: Wrong. Snowflake IDs are also time-ordered and largely predictable (timestamp plus machine plus sequence), and they can require 11 base62 characters, breaking the 7-character requirement.

options.text: Apply a bijective permutation to the counter (e.g. multiply by a constant sharing no factor with the code-space size and keep the remainder, understanding that this is only obfuscation) before base62-encoding.
options.explanation: Correct. A bijection (one-to-one mapping) over all 3.5 trillion 7-character values maps each counter value to a unique code, so it stays collision-free, and it can obscure the raw sequence, but a simple multiplier leaves a recoverable pattern. This guarantees uniqueness, not secrecy: at 10% occupancy random probes hit valid links about 10% of the time.

options.text: Rate limit the redirect endpoint so enumeration takes longer.
options.explanation: Wrong as the main fix. Rate limiting slows a single attacker, but distributed scrapers bypass it easily. It's a useful defence in depth, not a substitute for the collision-free seven-character mapping requested here.

questions.workedExample:
You want a one-to-one mapping over all seven-character values, preserving uniqueness while avoiding the raw sequential encoding. A simple multiplication has a recoverable pattern; use a vetted keyed permutation if hiding that relationship matters.

Simplest version:

```formula
f(n) = (an) mod 62^7
where
f: the bijective shuffle function applied before base62 encoding
n: the counter value, from 0 to 62^7 − 1
a: a constant that shares no factor with 62^7 (coprime with it): any odd number not divisible by 31, since 62 = 2 × 31
mod: modulo, the remainder after division, which wraps the result back into the 7-character range
62^7: the number of 7-character base62 codes, about 3.5 trillion
In words: multiply the counter by a fixed constant and keep the remainder; because the constant shares no factor with the space size, every counter value gets a different code.
```

This is a bijection, though the difference between decoded codes for known consecutive counters reveals the multiplier. A custom four-round Feistel recipe is omitted because no reviewed cryptographic construction is supplied. For private links use authorization or a properly designed longer capability token; a dense seven-character namespace is not adequate secrecy.

These concrete outputs are computed from the simple coprime multiplication fixture below, rather than arbitrary example strings. The permutation remains predictable from observed relationships and is unsuitable as access control.

```python
alphabet = (
    "0123456789"
    "abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz"
    "ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ"
)
def base62(n):
    if n == 0:
        return alphabet[0]
    chars = []
    while n:
        # Take the rightmost digit;
        # move left by dividing by 62.
        n, digit = divmod(n, 62)
        chars.append(alphabet[digit])
    return "".join(reversed(chars))

for counter in (1000001, 1000002):
    # Coprime multiplication preserves
    # uniqueness; it is not encryption.
    shuffled = ((1000003 * counter)
                % 62**7)
    print(base62(shuffled).zfill(7))
# hBy2Saf then hBy74jk: unique codes.
```

Codes remain unique and 7 characters, with no extra database reads.

lessons.title: Choose redirect caching and asynchronous analytics
lessons.summary: Choose Cache-Control explicitly for freshness and repeat click visibility.
lessons.body:
A redirect that is reused by a browser or edge cache may never reach the origin. This unit connects HTTP caching semantics to click visibility and the analytics pipeline.

## Deep dive 2: 301 vs 302

Both send the browser to the long URL. The difference is caching.

| | 301 Permanent | 302 Found |
|---|---|---|
| Heuristic cacheability | Yes | Not normally; explicit freshness can permit storage |
| Later clicks hit us? | Depends on freshness policy | Depends on freshness policy |
| Analytics | Cached visits may be missed | Cached visits may be missed |
| Updated target seen? | Depends on cache policy | Depends on cache policy |

A fresh cached redirect can bypass your service, hiding visits and delaying target or expiry changes. A **301** is heuristically cacheable; **302/307** can also be cached with explicit freshness. Use an explicit policy such as `Cache-Control: no-store` when repeat navigation should resolve through your service, and account for analytics delivery failures separately.

Without explicit cache headers, browsers treat a 301 as cacheable and may keep it indefinitely; a 302 is cached only if headers say so. A permanent redirect can still use a short freshness lifetime or `no-store`; the status and cache policy serve different purposes.

> [!note] Content gap: live provider headers
> Exact Bitly, t.co and TinyURL cache-header claims have been removed. No reproducible set of representative URLs and dated response captures was supplied, so this audit cannot reliably present those variable deployment settings as provider-wide facts.

So the real lever is `Cache-Control`, not only the status code. Say the trade-off explicitly; that's what the interviewer is checking.

## Deep dive 3: Analytics

Never update a counter row synchronously on every redirect. At 30,000 redirects/s, a popular link would become a hot row and add latency to every redirect.

Instead:

1. The redirect service emits a click event (`code, timestamp, country from IP, user agent, referrer`) to Kafka, fire-and-forget, and returns immediately.
2. A stream processor (Flink, Kafka Streams) aggregates events into per-link, per-hour buckets.
3. Aggregates go into an OLAP store such as ClickHouse or Druid, which answers "clicks by country last 7 days" quickly.

Raw events can also be written to object storage (S3) for reprocessing. If Kafka is briefly unavailable, the redirect must still work: buffer locally and drop analytics before you ever fail a redirect. Redirects are the product; analytics are a feature.

## Make the analytics guarantee explicit

Returning quickly and recording every click are competing requirements during a log outage. A fire-and-forget event can be lost between process failure and publication, even if Kafka itself is durable after acknowledgement. A bounded local queue needs a size limit, retention policy and metric for dropped events.

If the product requires durable click accounting, persist a recoverable event before acknowledging the operation or use an equivalent durable capture design, then measure its latency cost. For this availability-first shortener, redirect success takes priority and occasional missing analytics are accepted. Neither a 302 nor a no-store policy proves complete analytics: clients, bots and event delivery failures still need a measurement definition.

## Key takeaways

- Choose Cache-Control explicitly for freshness and repeat click visibility.
- Status codes and freshness policy are separate decisions.
- Keep analytics bounded and asynchronous; quantify tolerated event loss.

## Further reading

- [RFC 9111: HTTP caching](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9111.html)
- [RFC 9110: redirect status codes](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html)

questions.prompt: Your product manager wants accurate click counts and the ability to disable malicious links instantly. Which redirect status should the service return?

options.text: 301 Moved Permanently, because it is the standard for URL redirects.
options.explanation: Wrong as stated. Without cache headers, browsers may cache a 301 indefinitely, so repeat clicks never reach you and you can't reliably disable the link. Provider-wide header claims require current representative response captures, which are not supplied.

options.text: 404 Not Found, then let the browser search for the URL.
options.explanation: Wrong. 404 means the resource doesn't exist. It would break every link.

options.text: 200 OK with a page containing a JavaScript redirect.
options.explanation: Wrong. It works, but adds a full page load, breaks non-browser clients (curl, bots, some email clients) and harms SEO. Use a proper HTTP redirect.

options.text: 302 Found (or 307) with Cache-Control: no-store; enforce blocking on the redirect path and measure analytics delivery separately.
options.explanation: Correct. Explicit no-store avoids retaining this redirect in compliant HTTP caches. It cannot take back destinations already resolved by a client, guarantee click-event delivery, or instantly invalidate your own cache layers.

questions.workedExample: Choose an explicit cache policy. A 301 is heuristically cacheable; temporary redirects can also be cached with explicit freshness. For the stated control requirement, use 302/307 with `Cache-Control: no-store`, and make origin/edge blocking checks sufficiently fresh. Requests already redirected cannot be recalled. Click analytics also need delivery, deduplication and bot-counting rules; HTTP status alone cannot guarantee accurate counts. Exact provider cache settings are omitted because no reproducible dated captures are available.

questions.prompt: The redirect path must hold **p99 under 50 ms at 30,000 req/s** while also recording click analytics. Which design choices help? Select all that apply.

options.text: Publish a click event to Kafka asynchronously and return the redirect without waiting for the acknowledgement.
options.explanation: Correct. Decoupling analytics from the request path means the redirect's latency depends only on the lookup. If Kafka is slow, buffer or drop events rather than delay redirects.

options.text: Increment a `click_count` column in the links table on every redirect.
options.explanation: Incorrect. A synchronous write per redirect adds latency and creates hot rows for viral links, causing lock contention exactly when traffic is highest.

options.text: Read-through cache in Redis plus a short-lived negative cache for unknown codes.
options.explanation: Correct. Most lookups hit memory, and negative caching stops bots probing random codes from falling through to the database.

options.text: A small in-process LRU cache on each redirect server for the hottest links.
options.explanation: Correct. It avoids a network hop for viral links and protects the Redis shard that owns a hot key from saturating.

options.text: Use a 2PC transaction across the links store and the analytics store so both are always consistent.
options.explanation: Incorrect. Two-phase commit adds multiple round trips and blocks on the slowest participant. Analytics can be eventually consistent; a redirect must not wait on it.

questions.workedExample:
Budget the 50 ms:

| Step | Illustrative latency input, not a benchmark |
|---|---|
| In-process cache hit | < 0.1 ms |
| Redis hit | ~0.5–1 ms |
| KV store read | ~5–10 ms |
| Sync DB write | +5–20 ms, worse under contention |

Keep only reads on the critical path and push every write (analytics) off it. Layered caches handle hot keys; negative caching handles bots. Synchronous work can increase latency and contention; whether it violates 50 ms needs a representative load test.

lessons.title: Keep expiry and negative caching race-safe
lessons.summary: Check logical expiry on reads instead of waiting for physical deletion.
lessons.body:
The mapping store may replicate asynchronously, while redirect services cache both mappings and not-found results. This unit examines how those two optimisations can hide a new link and how to prevent that race.

## Deep dive 4: Caching and expiry

The application uses cache-aside: check Redis, read the store on a miss, then populate Redis. Links are effectively immutable, so cache invalidation is easy; set a TTL (say, 24 hours) and evict on expiry or deletion.

Two subtleties:

- **Negative caching.** Bots hammer random codes. Cache "not found" for a short time (60 s) so they don't all fall through to the database. A Bloom filter can reject absent codes only when it covers all committed codes relevant to that read; a stale filter must not suppress fresh links.
- **Expiry.** Check `expires_at` on every read (lazy expiry), and let a background job or the store's TTL feature (DynamoDB TTL, Cassandra TTL) physically delete rows later.

## Deep dive 5: Consistency after create

A subtle bug lurks between negative caching and replication. A user creates a link and pastes it into a chat; a friend clicks within 200 ms. If the redirect hits a replica (or another region) that hasn't received the write yet, it returns 404 and *caches the 404 for 60 seconds*. The link looks broken for a minute.

Fixes, roughly in order of preference:

- **Write-through on create.** The write API puts `code → long_url` into the cache as it writes the store, and deletes any negative entry for that code.
- **Fall back to the primary on a miss.** If the replica says "not found", retry against the primary (or home region) before caching a negative result. Misses on real codes are rare, so the extra cost is small.
- **Keep negative TTLs short** (seconds, not minutes) and only negatively cache after a cheap format rejection or a Bloom filter check whose completeness for relevant committed codes is guaranteed.

Immutable mappings simplify replication, but deletion, expiry, abuse blocking, custom-alias uniqueness and stale negative-cache fills still need consistency rules. A create racing with an older miss can be overwritten by a late negative fill; version or condition cache writes, or avoid negative caching valid-looking codes when strict freshness is required.

## Bottlenecks and trade-offs

- **Hot links**: in a scenario where a viral link gets over 100,000 requests a second, compare that load with measured shard capacity. Add a small in-process cache on each redirect server, or serve the redirect from the CDN edge.
- **ID coordinator**: range allocation makes it nearly irrelevant, but run it replicated (etcd/ZooKeeper) so block allocation survives a node loss.
- **Abuse**: shorteners are used to hide phishing links. Scan on creation, rescan periodically, and be able to disable a link globally (another reason to keep browser caching of redirects short).

## Key takeaways

- Check logical expiry on reads instead of waiting for physical deletion.
- A stale replica or Bloom filter must not hide a freshly created mapping.
- Version cache fills and combine hot-link caching with bounded blocking delays.

## Further reading

- [DynamoDB: time to live](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/TTL.html)
- [RFC 9111: HTTP caching](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9111.html)

questions.prompt: Users report that links they've *just* created sometimes 404 for about a minute, then start working. Redirects read from async replicas, and unknown codes are negatively cached for 60 s. What is happening, and what is the best fix?

options.text: The ID allocator is issuing duplicate codes; switch to Snowflake IDs.
options.explanation: Wrong. Duplicates would cause wrong redirects that never heal, not a 404 that fixes itself after a minute.

options.text: A click arrives before the replica has the new row, the 404 is negatively cached for 60 s, so the link looks broken until that entry expires. Write the mapping into the cache on create (clearing any negative entry), and check the primary before caching a 'not found'.
options.explanation: Correct. The 60-second healing time matches the negative-cache TTL, which is the giveaway. Write-through on create plus a primary fallback on a miss helps, but requires conditional/versioned cache fills so an older miss cannot overwrite the freshly created mapping.

options.text: Browsers cached a 301 for the old URL; switch to 302.
options.explanation: Wrong. The link is new, so no browser can have a cached redirect for it. The 404 comes from your own service.

options.text: Turn off negative caching altogether.
options.explanation: Partly works but overcorrects. Bots probing random codes would then all fall through to the database. Keep negative caching, but stop it caching false negatives for fresh links.

questions.workedExample:
Reconstruct the timeline:

```
at 0 s     create -> primary
at 50 ms  click -> replica: no row
        cache 'not found' 60 s
at 200 ms replica receives row
at 60 s   negative entry expires
```

Two ingredients help; neither alone proves correctness against all concurrent cache-fill races:

1. **Write-through on create**: set `code → url` in Redis and delete any negative key.
2. **Primary fallback**: on a replica miss, ask the primary before caching a negative result.

In interviews, linking a symptom's duration to a specific TTL is a strong debugging signal.

questions.prompt: A link in a Super Bowl advert gets **200,000 clicks/s** for ten minutes. It lives on one Redis shard that handles about 100k ops/s. Analytics for the advertiser matter. What is the best mitigation?

options.text: Re-shard Redis with more nodes so the key gets more capacity.
options.explanation: Wrong. Consistent hashing still places one key on one shard, so adding nodes doesn't spread a single hot key.

options.text: Return a 301 with no cache headers so browsers stop coming back.
options.explanation: Wrong for this case. Each viewer clicks once, so browser caching saves little, and you'd lose control of the link. Most of the 200k/s are different people.

options.text: Serve the redirect from the CDN edge or an in-process cache on every redirect server with a short TTL, and emit click events from there in batches.
options.explanation: Correct. Spreading the read across hundreds of edge locations or app servers takes it off the single shard, and a short TTL (seconds) bounds cache staleness and keeps control. Batched click logs preserve analytics.

options.text: Rate limit the link to 100k clicks/s.
options.explanation: Wrong. Dropping half the advertiser's traffic during their most expensive minute is the worst possible outcome.

questions.workedExample:
The bottleneck is one key on one shard, so the fix must **replicate the read**, not partition it further.

```formula
load = clicks / copies
load = 200,000/s / 300 ≈ 700/s
where
load: requests per second each cached copy serves
clicks: total clicks per second, 200,000
copies: edge locations or app servers holding the mapping, assumed about 300 ("hundreds")
/s: per second
≈: approximately equal to (rounded from 667)
In words: spreading 200,000 clicks a second over about 300 copies leaves each one only about 700 a second.
```

With a 5-second TTL, each copy is at most about 5 seconds stale.

Analytics can survive if batches are durably buffered/retried and duplicates handled; best-effort buffering can still lose events. In this design, edge workers or app servers log each click locally and ship counts in batches, rather than writing per click. The same idea (replicate hot keys, batch writes) applies to every hot-key question in this module.

lessons.title: Expand the namespace and preserve regional uniqueness
lessons.summary: Seven characters cannot hold ten years at a billion new links a day.
lessons.body:
Now increase the assumed workload tenfold: one billion new links a day and 300,000 redirects a second. Earlier units established cache freshness and non-reused ID ranges; apply both when expanding the namespace and serving regions.

## At 10x scale

At 1 billion new links a day and 300k redirects/s:

- **Seven characters is no longer enough** for 10 years (3.65 trillion links vs 3.5 trillion codes; see the sum below). Move to 8 characters (218 trillion) for new links. An 8-character string can never equal a 7-character one, so new generated links use exactly eight characters (left-pad short encodings), with a fresh permutation over all 218 trillion 8-character values. Also revise alias reservations or atomically skip already-claimed aliases.
- **Storage reaches petabytes** (about 1.8 PB raw over 10 years). Expire links nobody has clicked for years, or move them to cheaper storage.
- **Go multi-region.** Redirects are read-only and links are immutable, so replicate the links store asynchronously to every region and serve redirects locally. Give each region its own ID ranges so regions never need to coordinate on writes. A link created in Europe might take a second to resolve in Asia; the primary-fallback from deep dive 5 covers that window.
- **Push redirects to the edge.** CDN workers (Cloudflare Workers, Lambda@Edge) can hold hot mappings and reduce origin work; end-to-end latency still needs measurement, shipping click logs back in batches.
- **Shard the analytics pipeline** by code and pre-aggregate at the edge before sending upstream.

The two 10x sums:

```formula
links = 1 bn × 365 × 10 = 3.65 × 10^12
62^7 ≈ 3.52 × 10^12
storage = 3.65 × 10^12 × 500 B ≈ 1.8 PB
where
links: links created over 10 years at 1 billion a day
bn: billion (10^9)
62^7: the number of 7-character base62 codes
storage: raw bytes for those links at about 500 bytes each
B: bytes
PB: petabyte, 10^15 bytes (1,000 terabytes)
10^12: a trillion
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: ten years at a billion links a day needs slightly more codes than seven characters provide, and about 1.8 petabytes of raw storage.
```

## Distinguish generated codes from aliases

A region can create generated links during a bounded network partition while it still owns unused, durable ranges. It must stop or reject creation when its range is exhausted; disconnected regions cannot safely allocate the same new range. Custom aliases are different because a user can request the same text in two regions. Route that uniqueness decision to a home authority, or reject and defer alias creation while the authority is unreachable.

Asynchronous replicas support local redirect reads with a documented freshness delay. A fallback to the home region improves a fresh-link miss only when that region is reachable. Abuse blocking and deletions need a separate propagation or authoritative check policy; immutable destinations do not make these changes instantly consistent.

## Key takeaways

- Seven characters cannot hold ten years at a billion new links a day.
- Use an exact new code length and revisit alias reservations.
- Disjoint preallocated ranges support partitioned creation; custom aliases still need global uniqueness.

## Further reading

- [DynamoDB: conditional writes](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/Expressions.ConditionExpressions.html)
- [Python: numeric operations and divmod](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#divmod)

questions.prompt: Traffic grows 10x to **1 billion new links/day**, kept for 10 years, with 7-character codes. Which hard namespace-capacity problem follows directly from these numbers?

options.text: The ID coordinator can no longer keep up with block requests.
options.explanation: Wrong. At 1 billion links/day the peak is about 30,000 writes/s, so 1M-ID blocks are requested about 0.03 times a second, roughly once every 33 s overall. You can also simply make blocks bigger.

options.text: Base62 encoding becomes too CPU-intensive.
options.explanation: Wrong. Encoding takes a bounded number of divisions here; no measured CPU limit is supplied.

options.text: Redis can't hold the hot set.
options.explanation: Daily request count does not specify the number of distinct hot keys or their memory footprint. Trace the working set and benchmark capacity; no fixed 1 TB hot set follows from this prompt.

options.text: The 7-character code space runs out: 3.65 trillion links needed vs ~3.5 trillion codes available.
options.explanation: Correct. 1 billion × 365 × 10 = 3.65 trillion, slightly more than the 3.52 trillion 7-character codes, before counting wasted ranges. You need to move new links to 8 characters (218 trillion).

questions.workedExample:
Recompute the key estimate with the new numbers:

```formula
links = 1 bn × 365 × 10 = 3.65 × 10^12
space_7 = 62^7 ≈ 3.52 × 10^12
years = (3.52 × 10^12) / (3.65 × 10^11)
years ≈ 9.6
space_8 = 62^8 ≈ 2.18 × 10^14
where
links: links created in 10 years at 1 billion a day
bn: billion (10^9)
space_7, space_8: the number of 7- and 8-character base62 codes (7 or 8 copies of 62 multiplied together)
years: how long 7-character codes last at 365 billion (3.65 × 10^11) links a year
10^11, 10^12, 10^14: 1 followed by that many zeros
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: ten years at this rate needs 3.65 trillion codes but seven characters give only 3.52 trillion, so they run out in under ten years; eight characters give about 60 times the need.
```

You'd exhaust 7-character codes in about 9.6 years, sooner with waste. Moving to 8 characters gives about 218 trillion codes, about 60x headroom. An 8-character string can never equal a 7-character one, so you can switch with no migration: new generated links use exactly eight characters, including left-padding, and old codes keep working. Revise alias rules or use conditional inserts because existing custom aliases may already have eight characters.

The lesson: always re-run your capacity maths when the scale changes; a constraint that was 10x away can become binding.

questions.prompt: You expand to three regions so redirects are served locally. Generated-code link creation must remain available during a bounded partition while preallocated ID ranges remain; globally unique custom aliases are out of scope. Which choices fit? Select all that apply.

options.text: Give each region its own pre-allocated ID ranges, so regions generate codes without talking to each other.
options.explanation: Correct. Disjoint ranges guarantee uniqueness with no cross-region coordination, so a partitioned region can still create links.

options.text: Replicate the links table asynchronously to all regions.
options.explanation: Correct. Links are written once and never updated, so there are no conflicting writes to merge. Async replication keeps create latency local.

options.text: On a local miss, check the link's home region before returning 404.
options.explanation: Correct. It covers replication lag only when the home region is reachable; it cannot resolve an unknown link during that region's isolation. The home region can be encoded in the ID range, so you know where to ask.

options.text: Use a single global counter with synchronous cross-region consensus for every create.
options.explanation: Incorrect. Each create would pay a cross-region round trip (~100 ms), and a partitioned region couldn't create links at all, breaking the requirement.

options.text: Use 301 with an infinite cache so other regions are rarely asked.
options.explanation: Incorrect. It doesn't help create availability, and it gives up analytics and the ability to disable abusive links.

questions.workedExample:
Immutability is what makes this easy:

1. **Uniqueness without coordination**: region-specific ID ranges.
2. **Replication without conflicts**: rows never change, so last-writer-wins issues don't arise.
3. **Lag handling**: fall back to the home region on a miss.

Avoid putting anything cross-region and synchronous on the create path: it adds deployment-dependent network latency and may be unavailable in an isolated region. Disabling or deleting links still requires propagation rules even when destination mappings are immutable.

lessons.title: Set limiter guarantees and estimate capacity
lessons.summary: Separate policy targets from measured Redis capacity.
lessons.body:
A rate limiter caps how many requests a client can make in a period. It protects services from abuse and runaway clients, enforces pricing tiers ("free plan: 100 requests per minute"), and stops one tenant from starving everyone else.

On one server it's an in-memory counter. The interview is about making it work across hundreds of API servers, at a million requests a second, adding no more than a millisecond, and staying correct when clients race each other.

## Step 1: Requirements

**Functional**

- Limit requests per **key** (API key, user ID, IP address, or a combination) according to **rules** such as "100 requests/minute per API key on `POST /charges`".
- Support several rules per request (per-second burst limit *and* per-day quota).
- When a limit is exceeded, reject with **HTTP 429 Too Many Requests** and tell the client when to retry.
- Rules can be changed without redeploying.

**Non-functional**

- **Low overhead**: the check sits on every request, so it must add under ~1–2 ms at p99.
- **Highly available**: if the limiter is down, the API should keep working.
- **Approximately accurate**: a small overshoot (a few percent) is fine; massively over-admitting is not.
- **Distributed**: limits are global across all API servers, not per server.

## Step 2: Estimates

Assume an API fleet handling **1 million requests/s** at peak, with **10 million active keys** a day.

Every request needs one limiter check, which is one Redis call (a single Lua script). The number of Redis shards follows from dividing the check rate by what one shard handles:

```formula
shards = checks / cap
shards = 1,000,000/s / (50,000/s) = 20
where
shards: Redis shards (separate servers each holding part of the keys) needed, before adding replicas
checks: limiter checks per second, one per API request: 1 million at peak
cap: checks per second one shard handles at the target tail latency, here an assumed 50,000 (50k)
/s: per second
In words: a million checks a second at an assumed 50,000 per shard needs about 20 shards, plus replicas for failover.
```

Memory is keys times rules per key times bytes per counter:

```formula
memory = keys × rules × size
memory = 10M × 2 × 100 B ≈ 2 GB
where
memory: RAM needed for all counters
keys: active client keys per day, 10 million (10M)
rules: rules applied to each key, here 2 (a burst limit and a daily quota)
size: bytes per stored counter, an assumed 100 bytes (B)
M: million
B: bytes
GB: gigabyte, 10^9 bytes
≈: approximately equal to
In words: 10 million keys with two 100-byte counters each is about 2 GB of memory.
```

These are illustrative sizing inputs, not measured Redis capacity or memory bounds. Actual key strings, objects, allocator overhead, scripts, replication and network tails must be measured. A single atomic call reduces both race windows and network hops.

> [!note] Content gap: deployment benchmarks
> No reproducible deployment benchmark is supplied for the stated 1–2 ms target or per-shard throughput/footprint. Universal capacity and latency estimates are omitted; the calculation above uses explicit assumptions.

## Key takeaways

- Separate policy targets from measured Redis capacity.
- Count checks, active keys and rules independently.
- Choose the consequence of counter resets before selecting storage.

## Further reading

- [Stripe: rate and concurrency limiting](https://stripe.com/blog/rate-limiters)
- [Redis: benchmark limitations](https://redis.io/docs/latest/operate/oss_and_stack/management/optimization/benchmarks/)

questions.prompt: Your fleet handles **800,000 requests/s**. Each check is one Redis round trip, and a Redis shard comfortably handles **80,000 ops/s**. You want 50% headroom. How many primary shards do you need?

options.explanation: Wrong. 800k / 80k = 10 runs every shard at 100% with no headroom; any load skew or spike would push shards over capacity and blow your latency budget.
Wrong. 100 shards would run at 8k ops/s each (10% utilisation). It works but costs 5x what's needed. Over-provisioning is a legitimate choice, but it isn't what 50% headroom implies.
Wrong. 5 shards would each need 160k ops/s, twice their comfortable capacity.
Correct. With 50% headroom, each shard should run at about 40k ops/s. 800k / 40k = 20 shards.

questions.workedExample:
Headroom means running each shard below its comfortable maximum, so first find the target load per shard, then divide:

```formula
target = cap × (1 − headroom)
target = 80,000/s × 0.5 = 40,000/s
shards = load / target
shards = 800,000/s / (40,000/s) = 20
where
target: operations per second each shard should run at
cap: what one shard comfortably handles, 80,000 operations per second
headroom: the spare fraction to keep, 50% = 0.5
shards: primary shards needed
load: Redis calls per second, one per request: 800,000
/s: per second
In words: at half of its 80,000 capacity, each shard takes 40,000 checks a second, so 800,000 checks need 20 shards.
```

Add one replica each for failover: 40 Redis nodes in total.

Illustrative memory arithmetic, assuming 100 bytes per rule per key:

```formula
memory = 10M × 2 × 100 B = 2 GB
m_shard = 2 GB / 20 = 100 MB
where
memory: total counter memory for 10 million keys with 2 rules each
m_shard: memory each of the 20 shards holds
M: million
B: bytes
GB: gigabyte, 10^9 bytes
MB: megabyte, 10^6 bytes
In words: two gigabytes of counters split over 20 shards is about 100 MB each, before other overhead.
```

Measure actual memory before declaring throughput the limiting resource. If you also use local rejection caching (gateways remember "key over limit until a given time"), abusive clients stop generating Redis calls, so the real load is usually lower.

lessons.title: Choose identity, rule storage and shard routing
lessons.summary: Put checks before backend work and return useful retry guidance.
lessons.body:
## Step 3: API

The limiter is usually an internal service called by the API gateway, or a library or sidecar inside it. Lyft's open-source Envoy rate limit service is a gRPC service with essentially this shape:

```
ShouldRateLimit(domain, descriptors[])
  -> {overall: OK | OVER_LIMIT,
      statuses: [{limit, remaining,
                  resetSeconds}]}
```

To the *external* client, a rejected request looks like:

```
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 12
RateLimit-Limit: 100
RateLimit-Remaining: 0
RateLimit-Reset: 12
```

429 is defined in RFC 6585, and `Retry-After` is a standard HTTP header (RFC 9110). The `RateLimit-*` headers above are illustrative, non-standard field names from an earlier draft. The IETF HTTPAPI draft evolves structured quota fields; check the current draft rather than treating these names as a final standard. Many APIs still use their own `X-RateLimit-*` variants (GitHub sends `x-ratelimit-limit`, `-remaining` and `-reset`, the last as a Unix timestamp). Whatever the names, good headers matter: well-behaved clients back off instead of hammering you.

> [!warning] Retry storms
> If every rejected client retries exactly at the `Retry-After` time, they all come back in the same instant. Client SDKs should add random jitter to retries, and the server can vary `Retry-After` slightly per client.

## Step 4: Data model

Two kinds of data:

**Rules** are small, read constantly, changed rarely. Store them in a database or config repo and push them to every limiter instance, which caches them in memory.

Illustrative YAML configuration for this design, rather than an Envoy configuration format:

```yaml
# Identity and route choose the quota key.
domain: payments
key: api_key
path: /charges
# Capacity permits a burst of 100 requests.
capacity: 100
# Average allowance is 100 per 60 seconds.
refill_tokens: 100
refill_seconds: 60
algorithm: token_bucket
```

**Counters** are tiny, extremely hot and short-lived. Keep them in Redis (or Memcached), keyed by rule and client:

An illustrative Redis hash contains the balance and last refill time. These commands require a Redis connection; the timestamp is a fixture, not the current time.

```console
HSET rl:payments:/charges:{key_abc123} \
  tokens 37 last_refill 1727780000.123
HGETALL rl:payments:/charges:{key_abc123}
```

The hash contains 37 tokens and the supplied refill timestamp. Read, refill and decrement still need an atomic script; these two commands only demonstrate the stored representation.

The braces are a Redis Cluster **hash tag**: only the part inside `{}` is hashed to pick the shard. Tagging the *client* key puts all of one client's counters (burst limit, daily quota) on the same shard, so one Lua script can check several rules atomically, while different clients still spread across shards. Tagging the rule name instead (`{payments:/charges}`) would be a classic mistake: every client of that endpoint would land on one shard.

For this availability-first example, decide explicitly whether resetting counters is acceptable. A reset can grant a full new burst to every affected key, not merely a few percent overshoot. Security controls and billable quotas may require durable accounting or a different failure policy.

### Choosing the key

What you limit by matters as much as the algorithm:

- **API key or user ID** for authenticated traffic: precise and fair.
- **IP address** for anonymous traffic, with care. Thousands of mobile users can share one carrier-grade NAT address, and an IPv6 attacker can rotate through billions of addresses in a /64. Limit IPv6 by prefix (often /64) and set IPv4 limits loosely enough for shared addresses.
- **Combinations** for specific abuse: per (account, IP) limits on login can reduce some abuse, but distributed credential stuffing needs additional account/global signals and monitoring.

## Step 5: High-level design

```
 Client
   |
   v
 API gateway  <---- rules (cached,
   |   |              pushed on change)
   |   | check
   |   v
   | Limiter (lib/sidecar/svc)
   |   |
   |   v
   | Redis cluster
   | (counters, sharded by key)
   v
 Backend services
```

**Where to put it?**

- **In the client**: never trust it; clients can be modified.
- **In each service**: duplicated logic, inconsistent rules.
- **In the API gateway or a sidecar** (Envoy, Kong, AWS API Gateway): one place, before traffic reaches backends. This is the usual answer.
- **As a separate service** the gateway calls: centralises logic, costs an extra hop. Envoy's model is a sidecar that calls a central rate limit service backed by Redis.

## Key takeaways

- Put checks before backend work and return useful retry guidance.
- Hash-tag the client identity to co-locate its rules without one endpoint-wide hot shard.
- Consider NAT sharing, IPv6 rotation and retry jitter when choosing policy.

## Further reading

- [Envoy: global rate limiting](https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/intro/arch_overview/other_features/global_rate_limiting)
- [Redis: cluster hash tags](https://redis.io/docs/latest/operate/oss_and_stack/reference/cluster-spec/)
- [RFC 6585: HTTP 429](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6585)

questions.prompt: Your limiter runs on a 20-shard Redis Cluster. Counter keys look like `rl:{search}:user_123`. Dashboards show one shard at 100% CPU and the other 19 nearly idle, and most traffic is to `/search`. What's wrong?

options.text: Redis Cluster hashes the whole key, so `user_123` must be a hot user.
options.explanation: Wrong. When a key contains `{...}`, Redis Cluster hashes only the part inside the braces. One hot user wouldn't explain *all* search traffic landing on one shard.

options.text: The hash tag `{search}` sends every client's `/search` counter to the same slot. Tag the client instead, e.g. `rl:search:{user_123}`.
options.explanation: Correct. Only the tagged part picks the shard, so every key with `{search}` maps to one slot. Tagging the client spreads clients across shards and still co-locates one client's rules for multi-rule Lua scripts.

options.text: 20 shards is too few; add more.
options.explanation: Wrong. Adding shards can't help: all `{search}` keys map to the same hash slot, which lives on one shard however many you have.

options.text: Lua scripts are single-threaded, so one shard always does all the scripting.
options.explanation: Wrong. Each shard runs its own scripts on its own keys. The imbalance comes from key placement, not from Lua.

questions.workedExample:
Redis Cluster derives the slot from the key's first brace pair if that pair is non-empty:

```formula
slot = CRC16(tag) mod 16,384
where
slot: the hash slot, an integer from 0 to 16,383
CRC16: Redis Cluster's specified 16-bit cyclic redundancy check function
tag: the bytes inside the first non-empty brace pair; if the first opening brace has no closing brace or an empty pair, Redis hashes the entire key
mod: remainder after division
In words: keys with the same valid tag select the same slot; one primary owns that slot at a time.
```

```
rl:{search}:user_1   -> slot(search)
rl:{search}:user_2   -> slot(search)
rl:search:{user_1}   -> slot(user_1)
rl:search:{user_2}   -> slot(user_2)
```

The first scheme puts all search traffic on one shard. The second spreads by client while keeping `rl:search:{user_1}` and `rl:daily:{user_1}` together, so one script can check both atomically.

questions.prompt: You must rate limit an **unauthenticated** signup endpoint against bots, served to both IPv4 and IPv6 clients. Which practices are sound? Select all that apply.

options.text: Limit IPv6 clients by prefix (for example per /64) rather than per full address.
options.explanation: Correct. A single customer is often given a whole /64, so an attacker can rotate through billions of addresses in it. Limiting by prefix treats that block as one client.

options.text: Set IPv4 limits loosely enough that many users behind one carrier-grade NAT address aren't blocked.
options.explanation: Correct. Mobile carriers and offices put thousands of users behind one public IPv4 address. A tight per-IP limit there blocks real users.

options.text: Add a second, tighter limit keyed on something stronger, such as a device or session token, or require a CAPTCHA when per-IP limits trip.
options.explanation: Correct. Layering limits gives protection without relying solely on IPs, which are shared and spoofable at scale through proxies.

options.text: Trust a client-supplied `X-Forwarded-For` header from the internet as the client's IP.
options.explanation: Incorrect. Anyone can set that header. Only trust it when your own load balancer or CDN adds it, and read the address that your own infrastructure appended.

options.text: Fail open on this endpoint if the limiter is down, because availability always wins.
options.explanation: Incorrect for this case. Signup abuse protection is security-sensitive, like login. Failing closed (or falling back to a strict local limit) is the safer choice here.

questions.workedExample:
For anonymous endpoints the key is the hard part.

questions.prompt: A partner's batch job gets rate limited, and your server returns `Retry-After: 30` to each of its 5,000 worker threads. Exactly 30 seconds later, all 5,000 retry within the same 100 ms and are rejected again, over and over. What best fixes this?

options.text: Return `Retry-After: 0` so they retry immediately and spread out naturally.
options.explanation: Wrong. Immediate retries just turn the batch into a tight loop that hammers the limiter continuously.

options.text: Switch from 429 to 503 so clients treat it as an outage.
options.explanation: Wrong. 503 signals server unavailability rather than a client exceeding its quota, and many clients retry 503s more aggressively.

options.text: Add jitter: clients retry after `Retry-After` plus a random delay (and back off exponentially on repeated 429s), and the server can vary `Retry-After` slightly per request.
options.explanation: Correct. The synchronised wake-up is a thundering herd. Randomising retry times spreads 5,000 retries across a window, so they drain at the allowed rate instead of colliding.

options.text: Raise the partner's limit to 5,000 per burst.
options.explanation: Wrong as the fix. It might help this partner today, but the herd behaviour remains and returns at the next limit. Fix the retry pattern.

questions.workedExample:
Without jitter:

```
at 0 s   5,000 rejected, Retry-After 30
at 30 s  5,000 arrive in 100 ms
      bucket allows one burst, rest
      rejected
at 60 s  repeat
```

(Times are in seconds.) Now give each client a random extra delay:

```formula
d = 30 s + U(0, 30 s)
rate ≈ 5,000 / (30 s) ≈ 167/s
where
d: how long one client waits before retrying
U(0, 30 s): a random number drawn evenly (uniformly) between 0 and 30 seconds, different for each client
U: uniform random choice
rate: the expected average arrival rate of the retries
s: seconds; /s means per second
≈: approximately equal to
In words: spreading 5,000 retries evenly over a 30-second window brings them back at about 167 a second instead of all at once.
```

That rate is an expected average; actual admission still depends on the bucket rate, burst capacity and random variation. Exponential backoff on repeated 429s spreads them further. This is the same thundering-herd fix used for reconnect storms in chat systems.

lessons.title: Compare fixed windows with rolling-count estimates
lessons.summary: Fixed windows allow a double burst across an aligned boundary.
lessons.body:
A limiter rule might allow 100 requests per minute. The question is which minute: an aligned calendar interval or every possible rolling interval. This unit compares the counting algorithms before the next unit introduces a burst-and-average contract.

## Deep dive 1: Algorithms

### Fixed window counter

Count requests in each calendar window (`12:00:00–12:00:59`); reject once the count passes the limit. One `INCR` plus an `EXPIRE`.

- **Pro**: trivial, one integer per key.
- **Con: boundary bursts.** With a 100/min limit, a client can send 100 at 12:00:59 and 100 more at 12:01:00, so 200 requests in two seconds.

### Sliding request timestamp log

Store a timestamp for every request (a Redis sorted set). On each request, drop entries older than the window and count what's left.

- **Pro**: exact for the chosen rolling request-count interval when pruning, counting and recording accepted requests happen atomically.
- **Con: memory.** A limit of 10,000/hour stores up to 10,000 timestamps per key. At 10 million keys, that's prohibitive.

### Sliding window counter

Keep fixed-window counts for the current and previous window. A true rolling window ending now still overlaps the tail end of the previous window, so count the previous window in proportion to that overlap:

```formula
est = prev × (1 − t / w) + curr
est = 80 × (1 − 15 s / (60 s)) + 30
est = 80 × 0.75 + 30 = 90
where
est: the estimated number of requests in the last full window
prev: requests counted in the previous fixed window
curr: requests counted so far in the current window
t: time elapsed since the current window started, in seconds (s)
w: the window length, in seconds; here one minute = 60 s
t / w: the fraction of the current window that has passed, so 1 − t / w is the share of the previous window still inside the rolling window
s: seconds
In words: count the current window fully and the previous one only for the part that still falls inside the last minute; 25% into the minute, that is three quarters of the previous count.
```

So if the previous minute had 80 requests, the current has 30, and we're 25% through it, the estimate is 90. Under a limit of 100, allow.

- **Pro**: two integers per key, smooths boundary bursts.
- **Con**: approximate; it assumes requests in the previous window were evenly spread. Cloudflare reported around 0.003% incorrect decisions in its published workload. That historical empirical result is not a worst-case error bound; concentrated traffic can produce large errors.

## Key takeaways

- Fixed windows allow a double burst across an aligned boundary.
- Timestamp logs give exact counting semantics when implemented atomically.
- Two-window counters approximate a rolling interval and can err under concentrated traffic.

## Further reading

- [Cloudflare: measured sliding-counter approximation](https://blog.cloudflare.com/counting-things-a-lot-of-different-things/)
- [Redis: atomic increment and rate-limit patterns](https://redis.io/docs/latest/commands/incr/)

questions.prompt: A fixed window limiter allows **100 requests per minute** using windows aligned to the clock (`:00` to `:59`). What is the largest number of requests a client can get accepted in any 2-second span?

options.explanation: Wrong. That would be true for an exact rolling request-count interval. Fixed windows reset on the boundary, so a client can use two full allowances back to back.
Wrong. That's the average rate. A fixed window doesn't spread requests out; it only counts them per window, so a whole window's quota can arrive in a single second.

options.text: Unlimited
options.explanation: Wrong. The fixed window does cap each window at 100. The flaw is bounded: at most 2x the limit around a boundary.
Correct. 100 requests at 12:00:59 fill the first window; the counter resets at 12:01:00 and 100 more are allowed. That's 200 in about two seconds, double the intended rate.

Trace it:

12:01:00  window B starts at 0
12:01:00  100 reqs -> window B: 100

```

est = 100 × (1 − 0 s / (60 s)) + 0 = 100
where
est: estimated requests in the last 60 seconds
prev: requests in the previous window, 100
curr: requests so far in the current window, 0
t: seconds since the current window began, 0 at 12:01:00
w: the window length, 60 seconds
s: seconds
In words: at the very start of a new minute the whole previous minute still counts, so the estimate is already at the limit of 100.
```

So the second burst is rejected.

questions.prompt: A sliding window counter limits a key to **100 requests/minute**. The previous minute had **84** requests. We are **30 seconds** into the current minute, which has **55** requests so far. Is the next request allowed?

options.text: Yes: the estimate is 84 × (1 − 30/60) + 55 = 42 + 55 = 97, under 100.
options.explanation: Correct. Half the previous window still overlaps the trailing 60 s, so it contributes 42. 97 + 1 = 98 ≤ 100, so allow.

options.text: No: the estimate is 84 + 55 × (30/60) = 111.5, over 100.
options.explanation: Wrong. This weights the wrong window. The current window's count is used in full; it's the *previous* window that is scaled by how much of it still overlaps the trailing 60 seconds (1 − 30/60 = 0.5).

options.text: Yes, because only 55 requests have been made this minute.
options.explanation: Wrong. That's fixed-window logic. The sliding window counter also counts the share of the previous window that still overlaps the last 60 seconds.

options.text: No: 84 + 55 = 139, which exceeds 100.
options.explanation: Wrong. Adding both windows in full counts up to two minutes of traffic. The previous window must be weighted by its remaining overlap (here 50%).

The sliding window counter counts the current window in full and the previous window only for the share of it that still lies inside the last 60 seconds:

```formula
est = prev × (1 − t / w) + curr
est = 84 × (1 − 30 s / (60 s)) + 55
est = 84 × 0.5 + 55
est = 42 + 55 = 97
where
est: estimated requests in the trailing 60 seconds
prev: requests in the previous minute, 84
curr: requests so far this minute, 55
t: seconds elapsed in the current minute, 30
w: the window length, 60 seconds
s: seconds
In words: halfway through the minute, half of the previous minute still overlaps the trailing 60 seconds, so 42 of its 84 requests count, plus all 55 from this minute.
```

The new request would make 98, which is ≤ 100 (less than or equal to 100), so it is allowed and the current count becomes 56.

lessons.title: Implement burst limits with atomic refill checks
lessons.summary: Bucket capacity sets burst size; refill rate sets the long-run allowance.
lessons.body:
### Token bucket

Each key has a bucket that holds up to a fixed number of tokens and is topped up at a steady rate. Each request takes a token; an empty bucket means reject. Instead of a timer adding tokens, store just `tokens` and `last_refill` and work out the refill lazily on each request:

```formula
T_new = min(B, T + (now − last) × r)
where
T_new: tokens in the bucket after the refill, before this request takes one
T: tokens stored at the last update
B: the bucket capacity, the most tokens it can hold, which is the largest burst allowed
r: the refill rate, in tokens per second
now: the current time, in seconds
last: the time of the last update (last_refill), in seconds
now − last: seconds since the last update
min: "the smaller of", which stops the bucket filling beyond B
In words: add the tokens earned since the last request at r per second, but never more than the capacity B.
```

For a capacity of ten tokens and a refill rate of one token a second, substitute a bucket left with two tokens:

```formula
T_new = min(10, 2 + 5 s × 1/s) = 7
T_new = min(10, 2 + 60 s × 1/s) = 10
where
T_new: available tokens after refill and before spending one
min: choose the smaller value, capping at ten tokens
s: seconds; 1/s means one token per second here
In words: five idle seconds restore the bucket to seven tokens; a minute restores it only to its ten-token capacity.
```

The formula assumes the current time has not moved backwards. The Python fixture clamps negative elapsed time to zero; production timestamp persistence must also avoid granting the same elapsed interval twice after a clock regression.

```python
def refill(tokens, elapsed, cap, rate):
    # Clamp time if the clock regresses.
    earned = max(0, elapsed) * rate
    # Cap bursts after long idle time.
    return min(cap, tokens + earned)

print(refill(2, 5, 10, 1))
print(refill(2, 60, 10, 1))
# 7 then 10: refill stops at capacity.
```

This fixture checks refill arithmetic, not distributed admission. Production code must atomically update the token balance and timestamp and define how clock changes and failover are handled.

- **Pro**: allows controlled bursts (up to *B*) while enforcing a long-run average of *r*. Two numbers per key. Stripe’s published implementation describes this algorithm, and AWS API Gateway’s documentation specifies token-bucket throttling.
- **Con**: two parameters to tune; bursts are allowed by design, which might not suit a fragile downstream.

### Leaky bucket

Requests enter a FIFO queue drained at a fixed rate. Output is perfectly smooth, which suits traffic shaping in front of something fragile, but queued requests wait, and bursts are delayed rather than served. As a pure "allow or reject" meter, it behaves like a token bucket. GCRA (generic cell rate algorithm) is an elegant single-timestamp variant.

> [!tip] Default answer
> Token bucket for explicit burst-plus-average limits; sliding counters approximate rolling windows but do not provide exact rolling-window enforcement.

## Deep dive 2: Correctness under concurrency

Hundreds of gateway nodes check the same key at the same moment. A naive "read count, compare, write count + 1" is a race: two servers both read 99, both allow, both write 100, and the client got 101.

Fixes:

- **Atomic primitives.** For fixed windows, `INCR` is atomic and returns the new value: `INCR key`, then `EXPIRE key 60` on first creation, and compare the returned value with the limit. If the process dies between the two commands the key never expires, so do both in a Lua script or an appropriate transaction. Repeatedly extending a relative TTL changes expiration semantics unless the key includes the fixed window or the expiry is an absolute window boundary.
- **Lua scripts.** For token buckets, run the read-refill-decrement-write as a single Redis Lua script. Redis executes scripts atomically, so there are no races, and it's still one round trip.
- **Use the server's clock.** If every gateway passes its own `now`, clock skew between gateways distorts refills. Read time inside the script (`redis.call('TIME')`) so one clock is authoritative per key.

Redis Cluster maps keys to hash slots. The client-tag design co-locates that client's rules for one script; a global fleet counter or IP/account combination can require other slots, so arbitrary combined rules are not automatically atomic.

## Key takeaways

- Bucket capacity sets burst size; refill rate sets the long-run allowance.
- Perform read, refill, decrement and persistence in one atomic operation.
- Keep fixed-window expiry and clock semantics explicit.

## Further reading

- [Redis: atomic increment and rate-limit patterns](https://redis.io/docs/latest/commands/incr/)
- [Stripe: rate and concurrency limiting](https://stripe.com/blog/rate-limiters)
- [Redis: scripting atomicity](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/programmability/eval-intro/)

questions.prompt: Your API serves a mobile app that, on launch, fires **15 requests in under a second**, then is quiet. You want an average of **1 request/second** per user. Which algorithm fits best?

options.text: Fixed window of 1 request per 1-second window.
options.explanation: Wrong. It accepts at most one per fixed window (possibly two if the burst straddles a boundary), far short of the requested launch burst.

options.text: Leaky bucket draining 1 request/s.
options.explanation: Wrong. A leaky bucket smooths output to exactly 1/s, so the 15 launch requests would queue for up to 15 seconds, making the app feel broken.

options.text: Token bucket with capacity 20 and refill rate 1 token/s.
options.explanation: Correct. The bucket starts full, so the 15-request launch burst is served immediately, while the 1 token/s refill enforces the long-run average. This is exactly the burst-plus-average shape token buckets are designed for.

options.text: Sliding window log with a limit of 1 per second.
options.explanation: Wrong. It is exact, but exact enforcement of 1/s rejects the burst just as the fixed window does, and it costs more memory.

questions.workedExample:
A token bucket has two settings, and the lazy refill rule ties them together:

```formula
T_new = min(B, T + Δt × r)
T_new = min(20, 5 + 15 s × 1/s) = 20
where
T_new: tokens after refilling
T: tokens left after the last use, here 5
B: the capacity, the largest burst you will serve at once; the launch burst is 15, so 20 leaves room
r: the refill rate, the sustained average allowed, 1 token per second (1/s)
Δt: seconds since the bucket was last updated, here 15 s of quiet
min: "the smaller of", so the bucket never holds more than B
s: seconds
In words: after 15 quiet seconds at one token a second, the bucket is back to full.
```

Timeline: launch at time 0 takes 15 tokens (20 → 5). Over the next 15 s of quiet, the bucket refills to 20. A misbehaving client sending continuously gets at most 20 immediately, then 1 a second thereafter. That's why Stripe and AWS API Gateway use token buckets for API limits.

questions.prompt: Each of 200 gateway nodes implements the limit as: read the Redis count; if it is below the limit, separately write back one more and allow. Under load, clients exceed their limits. Why, and what's the fix?

options.text: Redis is losing writes; enable AOF persistence.
options.explanation: Wrong. Persistence affects durability across restarts, not concurrent correctness. The writes aren't lost; they overwrite each other.

options.text: Read-modify-write race: two nodes read the same value and both allow. Use an atomic operation (`INCR` and compare the returned value, or a Lua script).
options.explanation: Correct. Between GET and SET another node can read the same count. Redis executes `INCR` and Lua scripts atomically, so each request sees a unique, up-to-date count in one round trip.

options.text: The limit is too high; halve it to compensate.
options.explanation: Wrong. Halving the limit hides the bug inconsistently: overshoot depends on concurrency, so quiet clients are now over-restricted while busy ones still overshoot.

options.text: Use a distributed lock (e.g. Redlock) around each check.
options.explanation: Wrong as a first choice. A lock fixes the race but adds several round trips per request and becomes a bottleneck for hot keys. Atomic server-side operations solve it in one round trip.

questions.workedExample:
Interleave two gateways, A and B, with limit 100 and count 99:

```
A: GET -> 99   (99 < 100, allow)
B: GET -> 99   (99 < 100, allow)
A: SET 100
B: SET 100
```

Two requests allowed, count says 100: the client got 101. Fix:

A native Redis Lua script can combine the increment, first-key expiry and decision. The caller supplies an aligned-minute key as KEYS[1] and a limit such as 100 as ARGV[1].

```lua
-- KEYS[1] includes the aligned minute.
-- INCR returns the updated count.
local n = redis.call('INCR', KEYS[1])
if n == 1 then
  -- Expiry cleans up an old minute key.
  redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], 60)
end
local limit = tonumber(ARGV[1])
-- 1 allows; 0 rejects beyond the limit.
return n <= limit and 1 or 0
```

In a local Redis fixture with the count set to 99, successive calls return 1 then 0: request 100 is allowed and request 101 is rejected. This counts attempted requests, including rejections. The key’s minute identifier, rather than its cleanup TTL, defines the fixed window.

(Run the INCR and EXPIRE together in a Lua script; a plain MULTI cannot branch on the queued INCR result so a crash between them can't leave a key that never expires.)

For a token bucket, put refill + decrement in one Lua script so the whole step is atomic, and read time with `redis.call('TIME')` to avoid gateway clock skew.
