lessons.title: Bound fallback, leases and regional quota shares
lessons.summary: Choose fail-open or fail-closed from the consequence of excess work.
lessons.body:
## Deep dive 3: Failure and degradation

For ordinary availability-first quotas, limiter failure should not take the whole API down. Security-sensitive checks can require a stricter fallback.

- **Fail open.** If Redis times out (set an aggressive timeout like 5–10 ms), allow the request and emit a metric. Briefly over-admitting is better than rejecting all traffic.
- **Fail closed** only for limits that protect something critical, such as login attempts (brute-force protection) or expensive operations.
- **Local fallback.** Each gateway keeps an approximate in-memory bucket per key, sized as below. When Redis is unreachable, use that instead of nothing.

```formula
local = limit / G
local = 1,000/min / 50 = 20/min
where
local: the limit one gateway enforces on its own
limit: the global limit for the key
G: the number of gateways sharing the key's traffic, here an assumed 50
min: minute (/min means per minute)
In words: each gateway takes an equal slice of the global limit; it is only approximate, because a client's traffic is rarely spread evenly over gateways.
```

## Deep dive 4: Scaling the hot path

At a million checks a second, even one Redis round trip per request adds up. Options:

- **Local pre-check.** Gateways cache "this key is over limit until a given deadline" after a rejection, so a client hammering you is rejected locally without touching Redis.
- **Batching / token leasing.** A gateway takes, say, 10 tokens at a time from Redis and spends them locally. Ten times fewer Redis calls, at the cost of slight inaccuracy (unused leased tokens). Only lease for keys whose limit is much larger than the total that could be leased out at once (worked out below): with 200 gateways leasing 10 each, a 100/min customer's whole allowance would be stranded on 10 gateways while requests on the other 190 are rejected.
- **Hot keys.** One huge customer can concentrate load on one Redis shard. Splitting the key into sub-buckets (`key#0..key#7`, each with 1/8 of the limit, picked at random) spreads it. The cost is accuracy: a request can be rejected by an empty sub-bucket while others still have tokens, so this only suits customers whose traffic is large enough to average out.

The leasing rule and the sub-bucket split, as sums:

```formula
leased = G × lease
leased = 200 × 10 = 2,000 ≫ 100
sub = limit / 8
where
leased: the most tokens that could be held by gateways at once
G: the number of gateways, here 200
lease: tokens each gateway takes per Redis call, here 10
≫: much greater than
sub: the limit given to each of the 8 sub-buckets a hot key is split into
limit: the customer's total limit
In words: if the gateways together could lease far more than a customer's limit, leasing strands the allowance; splitting a hot key eight ways gives each piece an eighth of the limit.
```

## Deep dive 5: Multiple regions

Should a global limit of 1,000/min be enforced across US and EU together? Assume a cross-region round trip of about 100 ms in this scenario. Putting that round trip on each check would exceed the stated 1–2 ms overhead target. Actual network latency depends on deployment. Options:

- **Per-region limits**: give each region a share (e.g. proportional to its traffic). Simple, slightly unfair if traffic shifts.
- **Async sync**: each region enforces locally and gossips counts to the others every second or so. The global limit can be exceeded by roughly the traffic other regions admit during one sync interval. For a client sending near its limit that's a few percent; a client blasting all regions at once can overshoot by more, so pair this with a per-region burst cap.

Static regional shares can preserve a global quota if their allowances sum to the limit and redistribution cannot double-allocate. Asynchronous full-quota replicas instead need explicit overshoot and partition bounds.

## Key takeaways

- Choose fail-open or fail-closed from the consequence of excess work.
- Lease only when allowance is large enough to avoid stranding small quotas.
- Regional shares and asynchronously replicated full quotas have different overshoot guarantees.

## Further reading

- [Stripe: rate and concurrency limiting](https://stripe.com/blog/rate-limiters)
- [Cloudflare: measured sliding-counter approximation](https://blog.cloudflare.com/counting-things-a-lot-of-different-things/)

questions.prompt: The Redis cluster backing your limiter has a partial outage: 30% of checks time out. Assume ordinary API quota overruns are acceptable during this outage, while authentication abuse must remain bounded. Which responses fit that policy? Select all that apply.

options.text: Fail open for ordinary API limits: allow the request after a short timeout (~5–10 ms) and emit a metric.
options.explanation: Correct. The limiter exists to protect the API; rejecting 30% of legitimate traffic because the limiter is sick turns a partial limiter outage into an API outage.

options.text: Fail closed for login attempts and password resets.
options.explanation: Correct. These limits defend against brute-force attacks. Briefly rejecting some logins is less harmful than letting attackers try unlimited passwords while the limiter is down.

options.text: Fall back to per-gateway in-memory buckets sized at roughly limit ÷ number of gateways.
options.explanation: Correct. Local approximate limiting keeps some protection in place. It's inaccurate if load balancing is uneven, but far better than no limit at all.

options.text: Retry each timed-out Redis call up to 5 times before deciding.
options.explanation: Incorrect. Retries multiply load on an already struggling cluster and add tens of milliseconds to every request. Use short timeouts and a fallback, not aggressive retries.

options.text: Return 429 to every request until Redis recovers.
options.explanation: Incorrect. This blocks all customers, including well-behaved ones, making the limiter the cause of a total outage.

questions.workedExample:
Ask, for each limit: **what's worse, over-admitting or rejecting?**

| Limit | Worse outcome | Policy |
|---|---|---|
| API quota | Rejecting paying users | Fail open |
| Login attempts | Brute force | Fail closed |

Then layer a degraded mode: local buckets give partial protection with no network dependency. Avoid retry storms: a 5 ms timeout with zero retries targets a bounded network wait; scheduling, queueing and the fallback also contribute to measured tail latency while Redis recovers.

questions.prompt: A customer has a global limit of **10,000 requests/minute**, and you serve them from **US and EU** regions. A cross-region round trip is ~90 ms. Which design best balances accuracy and latency?

options.text: Each region enforces locally against a share of the limit; reserve shares so their sum stays within the quota and rebalance without double allocation.
options.explanation: Correct. Local enforcement avoids the 90 ms remote round trip. Static shares can preserve the total allowance but strand capacity in an idle region. Async full-quota replicas require separately justified overshoot bounds.

options.text: Every check in either region goes to a single US Redis cluster.
options.explanation: Wrong. EU requests would pay ~90 ms extra on every call, far over the 1–2 ms budget, and an Atlantic link problem would break EU rate limiting entirely.

options.text: Use a synchronously replicated multi-region database with strong consistency for counters.
options.explanation: Wrong. A commit quorum spanning these regions requires cross-region coordination; the supplied 90 ms round trip would exceed this check's budget. Quorum placement and the client's region determine which requests pay that delay. Strong consistency is overkill for a counter where a few percent overshoot is acceptable.

options.text: Give each region the full 10,000/min limit independently.
options.explanation: Wrong. The customer could get up to 20,000/min, a 100% overshoot. That's a pricing and protection failure, not an acceptable approximation.

questions.workedExample:
Quantify the overshoot of the async option. With a 1-second sync interval, the overshoot is roughly what the other region admits before the next sync:

```formula
rate = 10,000 / (60 s) ≈ 167/s
over ≈ rate × t_sync = 167/s × 1 s = 167
share = over / limit
share = 167 / 10,000 ≈ 1.7%
where
rate: the customer's limit as a per-second rate
over: extra requests admitted beyond the limit before the regions next exchange counts
t_sync: the sync interval, 1 second
share: the overshoot as a fraction of the per-minute limit
limit: the global limit, 10,000 requests per minute
s: seconds; /s means per second
≈: approximately equal to
In words: a client sending at its limit can slip about one second of extra traffic through, roughly 2% of its per-minute limit.
```

If both regions admit a second's worth, the overshoot is up to about 333, around 3%. So for a client sending at about its limit the overshoot is roughly 167–333 requests, or 2–3% of the limit.

A client blasting both regions far above its limit can overshoot by more within that second, which is why the async scheme is usually paired with a per-region per-second cap.

Compare that with adding 90 ms to every EU request. Acceptable overshoot is a policy choice; gossip alone gives no small bound during an extended partition. The static-split variant (e.g. US 6,000, EU 4,000) is simpler still but unfair when traffic shifts between regions.

questions.prompt: To save Redis calls, each of **200 gateways** leases **10 tokens** at a time from a client's central bucket. A small customer has **100 tokens available in the current window**, with no refill during this burst and no outstanding earlier leases. Their traffic is spread evenly across all gateways. What goes wrong?

options.text: Nothing: leasing is always accurate because tokens are only spent once.
options.explanation: Wrong. Tokens are spent once, but where they sit matters. Leased tokens are stranded on whichever gateways took them.

options.text: The customer gets 2,000 requests/minute because each gateway gets its own 10.
options.explanation: Wrong. Leases come out of the central bucket, so only 100 tokens are available in this stated window. The problem is the opposite: under-admission.

options.text: The first 10 gateways to ask take all 100 tokens; requests landing on the other 190 gateways are rejected even though most leased tokens sit unused.
options.explanation: Correct. Leasing only works when the limit is large compared with the lease size times the number of gateways. Here 10 × 200 = 2,000 tokens would be needed to give every gateway one lease; the customer has 100.

options.text: Redis load increases, because leasing adds a call per request.
options.explanation: Wrong. Leasing reduces Redis calls; that's its purpose. The issue is accuracy for small limits.

questions.workedExample:
Compare lease capacity with the limit:

```formula
leased = G × lease = 200 × 10 = 2,000
served = limit / lease = 100 / 10 = 10
where
leased: tokens needed to give every gateway one lease
G: the number of gateways, 200
lease: tokens per lease, 10
limit: tokens the customer has this window, 100
served: how many gateways can get a lease before the tokens run out
In words: one lease for every gateway would need 2,000 tokens, but the customer's 100 tokens cover only 10 gateways.
```

Before any further refill or window reset, only 10 of the 200 gateways can obtain a lease. With traffic spread evenly, 190 / 200 = 95% of requests hit a gateway with no tokens.

Fixes:
- Lease only for keys whose limit is much larger than the gateway count times the lease size (e.g. limits above ~100k/min).
- Scale the lease size with the limit (e.g. 1% of it).
- Use direct Redis checks for small keys, which are low-traffic anyway.

lessons.title: Protect in-flight work and total fleet capacity
lessons.summary: Per-client rates cannot bound all fleet traffic or long-running work.
lessons.body:
Earlier units bound request counts for each client. A service can still overload when many compliant clients arrive together, or when a few allowed requests run for a long time. This unit separates admission rate from resource occupancy.

## Bottlenecks and trade-offs

| Choice | Trade-off |
|---|---|
| Central Redis | Accurate, +1 hop |
| Local only | Fast, inaccurate |
| Fail open | Available, abusable |
| Fail closed | Safe, fragile |

Also mention that rate limiting is not load shedding. Stripe, for example, runs request-rate and concurrency limiters per user *and* fleet-wide load shedding mechanisms that drop low-priority traffic when the whole system is under strain. Per-key limits don't protect you when a million well-behaved clients all arrive at once.

Rate is also not the same as work in progress. Little's law, a general result for any stable queueing system, links them:

```formula
L = λ × W
L = (100 / (60 s)) × 20 s ≈ 33
where
L: the average number of requests in flight (started but not finished)
λ: lambda, the average rate of accepted arrivals, here 100 per minute = 100 / 60 s ≈ 1.67 per second
W: the average time each request takes, in seconds, here 20 s
s: seconds
≈: approximately equal to
In words: in-flight work equals how fast requests arrive times how long each one stays.
```

So a customer within a 100/min limit on a 20-second report endpoint holds about 33 requests in flight, even though the rate limit is respected. Little's law holds only for long-run averages in a stable system (one that keeps up with its arrivals). A **concurrency limiter** (a cap on in-flight requests per customer, say 10) bounds that directly.

## At 10x scale

At 10 million checks/s:

- A central Redis call per request may become expensive; shard count follows a representative script benchmark. Move to **two-tier limiting**: gateways enforce locally with leased tokens and sync with Redis every ~100 ms.
- Push coarse limits (per-IP DDoS protection) to the **edge/CDN** so abusive traffic never reaches your data centre.
- Use **per-region** limits, with periodic rebalancing of each region's share.
- Treat rule changes as a deployment: version them, roll them out gradually, and have a kill switch, because a wrong rule can reject all traffic instantly.

## Key takeaways

- Per-client rates cannot bound all fleet traffic or long-running work.
- Little’s law relates stable long-run averages, not instantaneous concurrency.
- Use concurrency caps, load shedding and gradual rule deployments.

## Further reading

- [Stripe: rate and concurrency limiting](https://stripe.com/blog/rate-limiters)
- [MIT: Little’s law](https://web.mit.edu/1.041/www/lectures/L3-cumulative-diagram-2026sp.pdf)

questions.prompt: Every customer is within their 100 requests/minute limit, yet the API falls over. A heavy report endpoint takes ~20 s per call, and a sales event has tripled overall traffic. Which mechanisms directly bound concurrent work or shed aggregate overload? Select all that apply.

options.text: A per-customer **concurrency limiter** (for example, at most 5 in-flight report requests).
options.explanation: Correct. Request-rate limits don't cap how much work is in progress. At 100/min with 20 s each, one customer can hold ~33 requests in flight; a concurrency cap bounds that directly.

options.text: A fleet-wide **load shedding** mechanism that drops low-priority traffic when total utilisation is too high.
options.explanation: Correct. Per-key limits can't protect you when every client is individually well-behaved but the total exceeds capacity. Stripe runs fleet-level load shedding mechanisms for exactly this.

options.text: Lower every customer's per-minute limit by half.
options.explanation: Incorrect. It punishes all customers permanently for a temporary capacity problem, and still doesn't bound slow, concurrent work.

options.text: Move the rate limiter from the gateway into each backend service.
options.explanation: Incorrect. Moving the limiter doesn't change what it measures. The gap is concurrency and overall capacity, not limiter placement.

options.text: Prioritise critical traffic (e.g. payments) over less critical (e.g. reports) when shedding.
options.explanation: Correct. Shedding by priority keeps the most important requests flowing while the system is overloaded.

questions.workedExample:
Little's law links stable averages: mean in-flight work is the accepted arrival rate multiplied by mean duration. It is not a hard instantaneous concurrency cap.

```formula
L = λ × W
λ = 100 / (60 s) ≈ 1.67/s
L = 1.67/s × 20 s ≈ 33
where
L: average requests in flight (started, not finished)
λ: lambda, the average accepted arrival rate per customer: 100 per minute
W: average time per request, 20 seconds
s: seconds; /s means per second
≈: approximately equal to
In words: a customer sending 100 slow requests a minute keeps about 33 of them running at once.
```

That's per customer, all within the rate limit. So you need:

1. **Concurrency limits** per customer for slow endpoints.
2. **Fleet-wide load shedding** for aggregate overload.
3. **Priorities** so shedding drops the least important work first.

Stripe's write-up describes exactly this layering: request-rate limiter, concurrency limiter, and two kinds of load shedding mechanism.

lessons.title: Size suggestion traffic and snapshot memory
lessons.summary: Debouncing changes the number of requests per search.
lessons.body:
Type "how to" into a search box and suggestions appear before you finish the word. Every keystroke is a request, so a search engine's autocomplete gets several times the traffic of search itself, and each response must arrive before the user types the next character.

The trick to this problem is realising that **the serving path should do almost no work**. All the expensive thinking (counting, ranking, filtering) happens offline, and the online path is a lookup.

## Step 1: Requirements

**Functional**

- Given a prefix, return the top **k** (say 10) completions.
- Rank by popularity, with some weight for recency so trending queries appear.
- Support multiple languages/locales.
- Never suggest offensive, dangerous or private content.

**Non-functional**

- **Latency**: assume a character every 100–200 ms for this interaction budget. Suggestions should render within ~100 ms end to end, so the server budget is ~10–20 ms.
- **Availability**: if autocomplete is down, search still works, so it's important but not critical. Degrade gracefully (show nothing) rather than slow the search box.
- **Freshness**: a new trending query (breaking news) should appear within minutes to an hour; general popularity can update daily.
- **Eventual consistency** is fine: two users seeing slightly different suggestions is harmless.

Out of scope: spelling correction, full search results.

## Step 2: Estimates

Assume **1 billion searches/day**. Users type ~20 characters per query, but clients **debounce** (wait ~100 ms of idle before sending) and stop once they pick a suggestion, so call it **~6 suggestion requests per search**.

Requests per second are searches per day times requests per search, divided by the seconds in a day:

```formula
rate = 1B × 6 / (10^5 s) ≈ 60,000/s
peak = 60,000/s × 3 = 180,000/s
where
rate: average suggestion requests per second
peak: requests per second at the busiest time, using an assumed peak factor of 3
B: billion (10^9) searches per day
6: suggestion requests per search after debouncing
10^5: 100,000, the seconds in a day (86,400) rounded up
s: seconds; /s means per second
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: a billion searches a day at six requests each is about 60,000 requests a second on average, and three times that at peak.
```

What to store? Most queries are rare; the long tail is huge and mostly useless for suggestions. Keep the **top ~100 million queries** by frequency.

Size the three parts of the index: the query strings, the trie nodes (one per distinct prefix), and a top-10 list at every node:

```formula
strings = 100M × 25 B ≈ 2.5 GB
max nodes = 100M × 20 = 2 bn
nodes ≈ 500M
lists = 500M × 10 × 4 B = 20 GB
where
strings: bytes to store the query text itself
max nodes: the most trie nodes possible, if no two queries shared a prefix
nodes: the assumed number of trie nodes once shared prefixes are counted once
lists: bytes for a top-10 list of 4-byte query IDs at every node (40 bytes per node)
M: million (10^6)
bn: billion (10^9)
B: bytes
GB: gigabyte, 10^9 bytes
≈: approximately equal to (rounded or assumed)
In words: the query text is small; the per-node top-10 lists dominate, at about 20 GB, and with overhead the whole index is assumed to be 30–50 GB.
```

(The node count is an assumption: with no sharing at all, 100M queries capped at 20 characters would need up to 2 billion nodes, but popular queries share long prefixes heavily.) A 4-byte ID is enough because 4 bytes is 32 bits:

```formula
2^32 ≈ 4.3 × 10^9 > 10^8
where
2^32: the number of different values 32 bits can hold, 32 copies of 2 multiplied together
10^9: a billion; 10^8: a hundred million, the number of queries kept
>: is greater than
≈: approximately equal to
In words: 32 bits can number about 4.3 billion things, far more than the 100 million queries to identify.
```

Under these compact-layout assumptions, the index may fit in one large machine's RAM. Measure the built representation: pointers, child maps, strings and allocator overhead can make a naive trie much larger. We'll replicate it rather than shard it, which keeps serving simple. Budget for **two copies** in memory, because a node loads the new trie snapshot before releasing the old one: a 50 GB index wants a machine with well over 100 GB of RAM.

## Key takeaways

- Debouncing changes the number of requests per search.
- Measure the built index; a query count does not prove its memory footprint.
- Budget for old and new snapshots to coexist while readers finish.

## Further reading

- [Finite-state transducers and compact indexes](https://burntsushi.net/transducers/)
- [Elasticsearch: completion suggesters](https://www.elastic.co/docs/reference/elasticsearch/rest-apis/search-suggesters)

questions.prompt: You get **2 billion searches/day**. With debouncing, each search generates about **5** suggestion requests. What is the approximate **peak** suggestion request rate, assuming peak is 3x average?

options.text: About 35,000/s
options.explanation: Wrong. 35,000/s is the average rate for about 3 billion requests a day. You've likely missed the peak factor and part of the requests-per-search multiplier.

options.text: About 100,000/s
options.explanation: Wrong. That's the average rate. You must size the serving fleet for peak traffic, about 3x higher.

Wrong. This is 10x too high: a 3M/s peak implies a 1M/s average, or about 86 billion requests a day, perhaps from counting a request for every keystroke of ~20-character queries and then applying the peak factor twice.

options.text: About 300,000/s
options.explanation: Correct. 2 billion × 5 = 10 billion requests/day; 10 billion / 100,000 s ≈ 100,000/s average (about 116,000 using the exact day length); × 3 ≈ 300,000–350,000/s at peak.

questions.workedExample:
Multiply searches by requests per search, divide by the seconds in a day, then apply the peak factor:

```formula
daily = 2B × 5 = 10B
avg = 10B / (86,400 s) ≈ 115,700/s
quick = 10B / (10^5 s) ≈ 100,000/s
low = 3 × 100,000/s = 300,000/s
high = 3 × 115,700/s ≈ 350,000/s
where
daily: suggestion requests per day
avg: the exact average requests per second
quick: the same using 1 day ≈ 100,000 s
low, high: peak requests per second (3 times the average) from the rounded and the exact average
B: billion (10^9)
10^5: 100,000
s: seconds; /s means per second
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: 10 billion requests a day is about 100,000–116,000 a second on average, roughly 300,000–350,000 at peak.
```

What it implies: assuming a benchmark demonstrates 1,000 req/s per core at the target latency, that is ~350 cores at peak, i.e. a few dozen servers before caching. A CDN serving short prefixes typically absorbs a large share of this, so the origin fleet can be much smaller.

questions.prompt: Your offline-built trie, with top-10 precomputed at each node, is **40 GB**. You serve 300k req/s across three regions. How should you deploy it?

options.text: Replicate the full trie in memory on every serving node, in every region, and scale by adding replicas.
options.explanation: Correct. 40 GB fits comfortably in RAM on a standard large instance. Full replication means any node can answer any prefix, there's no cross-shard routing, and additional replicas increase capacity until shared network, deployment or load-balancing limits intervene.

options.text: Store it in a relational database and query it with `LIKE 'prefix%'`.
options.explanation: Wrong. A B-tree index can find matching rows for a prefix, but ranking millions of matches per request is far too slow, and it ignores the precomputed top-k entirely.

options.text: Shard it alphabetically across 26 servers, one per first letter.
options.explanation: Wrong. Alphabetical sharding is badly skewed (far more queries begin with 's' or 'c' than 'x' or 'q'), and it's unnecessary because 40 GB fits on one machine.

options.text: Keep it in object storage and read the relevant node on each request.
options.explanation: Wrong. Object storage reads take tens of milliseconds each, consuming the whole latency budget for a single lookup. Object storage is where trie snapshots are published, not served from.

questions.workedExample:
Decision process:

1. **Does it fit in RAM?** 40 GB on a 128 GB machine: yes, with room for two versions during a swap (80 GB).
2. **If it fits, replicate.** Sharding adds routing, load skew and partial-failure modes; it's only worth it when data doesn't fit.
3. **Size the fleet**, with an explicitly assumed 1,000 req/s per core:

```formula
cores = 300,000/s / (1,000/s) = 300
nodes = 300 / 32 ≈ 10
where
cores: CPU cores needed at full use
nodes: servers needed if each has 32 cores
/s: per second
≈: approximately equal to (9.4 rounded up)
In words: 300,000 requests a second needs about 300 cores, or about ten 32-core machines.
```

Assuming balanced regional traffic, four nodes per region give spare capacity for a node loss in this input model. To sustain all 300,000 requests/s after losing one of three equal regions, five 32-core nodes per region leave 320 cores in the two surviving regions. Validate load redistribution and shared dependencies as well.

Shard (by locale first, then by hashed prefix) only when the index outgrows a single machine.

lessons.title: Precompute prefix answers and control client requests
lessons.summary: A top-k list at each prefix removes subtree search from serving.
lessons.body:
## Step 3: API

```
GET /v1/suggest?q=how%20to%20m
              &locale=en-GB&limit=10
-> 200
{ "prefix": "how to m",
  "suggestions": [
    "how to make pancakes",
    "how to meditate", ...] }
Cache-Control: public, max-age=300
```

Client behaviour matters as much as the server:

- **Debounce** keystrokes (~100 ms) so fast typists don't send a request per character.
- **Cancel** in-flight requests when a newer prefix is typed, and ignore stale responses that arrive out of order.
- **Cache locally**: if the user deletes a character, the previous prefix's results are already in memory.
- **Filter locally**: if the suggestions for "how to m" are known, the client can filter them for "how to ma" as provisional results, but that subset may omit the true top completions for the longer prefix; fetch again when complete results matter.

## Step 4: Data model

### The trie

A [trie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trie) stores strings by their characters, one level per character, so all strings sharing a prefix share a path.

```
        (root)
        /    \
       h      t
       |      |
       o      r
      / \     |
     w   t    e
     |   |    |
    ...  e    e
         |
         l
```

A naive lookup walks to the prefix node, one step per character, then searches the entire subtree for the most popular completions. For a short prefix like "s", that subtree contains millions of queries, which is far too slow.

### Precompute top-k at every node

Store the top-k completions **at each node**. Lookup becomes "walk to the node, return its list". Big-O notation describes how the work grows:

```formula
naive = O(p + S)
precomputed = O(p + k)
where
O(...): Big-O, "grows at most in proportion to" the expression inside, ignoring constant factors
p: the length of the typed prefix, in characters
S: the number of nodes in the subtree below the prefix, which can be millions for a one-letter prefix
k: the number of suggestions returned, here 10
naive, precomputed: the lookup cost without and with a top-k list stored at each node
In words: storing the answer at each node turns a search of a possibly huge subtree into a walk of a few characters plus reading k items.
```

That is, plus output-string bytes, with no subtree search.

```
node "how t" -> [how to tie a tie (98k),
                 how to train your dragon,
                 ...]
```

The cost is memory (k entries per node) and rebuild work, but we do that offline. Use compact IDs instead of full strings in each list, and cap prefix depth (beyond ~20–30 characters, there's little to suggest).

### Alternatives

- **Flattened trie in a KV store**: store `prefix → top-k list` directly in Redis or Cassandra. Easy to shard and update; memory relative to a trie depends on key duplication and representation. Good if the index outgrows one machine.
- **Finite-state transducers**: Lucene and Elasticsearch's completion suggester use FSTs, a compressed trie that shares suffixes as well as prefixes, often several times smaller.
- **Radix trees** collapse chains of single-child nodes into one edge, saving memory for long unique tails.

## Step 5: High-level design

```
 Browser/app (debounce, cache)
        |
        v
 CDN edge cache
        |  (miss)
        v
 Suggest service x N
 (whole trie in RAM)
        ^
        | load snapshot
 Object store (trie files)
        ^
        | build
 Trie builder (batch)
        ^
        | query counts
 Aggregator (stream + batch)
        ^
        |
 Search logs -> Kafka
```

Two separate paths:

- **Serving path** (top half): read-only, in memory, cached at the edge.
- **Data path** (bottom half): logs → counts → ranked lists → a new trie snapshot every hour or day.

They meet only at the snapshot. The suggest service never writes anything.

## Key takeaways

- A top-k list at each prefix removes subtree search from serving.
- Debounce, cancel, ignore stale responses and reuse local results.
- Keep the serving path separate from the snapshot-building pipeline.

## Further reading

- [Meta: the life of a typeahead query](https://engineering.fb.com/2010/05/17/web/the-life-of-a-typeahead-query/)
- [Elasticsearch: completion suggesters](https://www.elastic.co/docs/reference/elasticsearch/rest-apis/search-suggesters)
- [Trie data structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trie)

questions.prompt: In a plain trie (no precomputation), why is finding the top 10 completions for the prefix `s` slow?

options.text: Walking from the root to the node for `s` takes time proportional to the number of stored queries.
options.explanation: Wrong. Reaching the prefix node takes one step per character of the prefix, here a single step. The walk is cheap; what follows isn't.

options.text: Tries can't store popularity scores, so you must query a database for each candidate.
options.explanation: Wrong. Nodes can store any payload, including a score on terminal nodes or a precomputed top-k list. The slowness comes from the traversal, not from missing data.

options.text: The lookup must traverse the whole subtree under `s`, potentially millions of queries, to find the 10 most popular.
options.explanation: Correct. Every query starting with `s` lives below that node. Without precomputed results you have to visit them all (or a large part) and pick the top 10, which is far too slow for a 10–20 ms budget.

options.text: Single-character prefixes cause hash collisions in the trie.
options.explanation: Wrong. Tries aren't hash tables; each character selects a child edge. There's no collision concept here.

questions.workedExample:
Split the lookup into two phases:

1. **Find the prefix node**: one step per character. For `s`, that is one step.
2. **Collect completions**: visit every terminal node in the subtree and keep the best 10. For `s`, that's millions of nodes.

In Big-O terms:

```formula
plain = O(p + S)
precomputed = O(p + k)
where
O(...): Big-O, "grows at most in proportion to" what is inside, ignoring constant factors
p: the prefix length in characters; for "s", p = 1
S: the number of nodes in the subtree under the prefix, millions for "s"
k: the number of suggestions returned, 10
plain, precomputed: lookup cost without and with a stored top-k list at each node
In words: a plain trie pays for the whole subtree; storing the top 10 at each node leaves only the short walk plus reading 10 items.
```

Phase 2 dominates. The fix is to **precompute** the top-10 list at every node during the offline build, so phase 2 becomes "return the stored list". The cost is then O(p + k) plus output-string bytes, conventionally written O(p) only when output size is treated as fixed.

questions.prompt: Which client-side behaviours reduce load or improve perceived latency for typeahead? Select all that apply.

options.text: Debounce keystrokes, sending a request only after ~100 ms of no typing.
options.explanation: Correct. Fast typists produce several keystrokes within 100 ms; debouncing collapses them into one request, cutting load substantially.

options.text: Cache responses by prefix in memory so backspacing reuses earlier results.
options.explanation: Correct. Deleting a character returns to a prefix that was just fetched, so a local cache answers instantly with no network call.

options.text: Ignore responses for prefixes older than the current input.
options.explanation: Correct. Responses can arrive out of order; rendering a stale one makes suggestions flicker to an older prefix. Dropping them (or cancelling the request) keeps the UI correct.

options.text: Retry failed suggestion requests three times with exponential backoff.
options.explanation: Incorrect. By the time a retry succeeds, the user has typed more characters, so the result is useless. For typeahead, a failed request should simply be dropped.

options.text: Send a request for every keystroke so suggestions are always current.
options.explanation: Incorrect. This multiplies load for almost no benefit, since intermediate prefixes are usually never seen by the user.

questions.workedExample:
Think about a user typing "pancakes" quickly (8 characters in ~800 ms):

- **No debounce**: 8 requests.
- **100 ms debounce**: request count depends on gaps between keystrokes; a continuous 100 ms cadence can send nearly every character, while shorter gaps coalesce.
- **Backspace** from "pancakes" to "pancake": a cache hit only if that prefix was previously fetched; debouncing may have skipped it.
- **Out-of-order arrival**: "pan" results arrive after "pancak" results; ignoring them avoids a visible flicker.

Retries make no sense for data with a lifespan of a few hundred milliseconds.

lessons.title: Build fresh suggestions without exposing rare queries
lessons.summary: Rank submitted searches with explicit decay and eligibility rules.
lessons.body:
## Deep dive 1: The data collection pipeline

1. **Log** every submitted search (not every keystroke; we rank on what people *searched*) with timestamp, locale and a pseudonymous user ID (which is not automatically anonymous). At 1B/day, sampling 1 in 10 still gives plenty of signal for popular queries.
2. **Aggregate** with a stream processor (Flink, Kafka Streams) into counts per `(query, locale, hour)`. For truly huge streams, approximate structures such as a [count-min sketch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count%E2%80%93min_sketch) with a heavy-hitters heap find frequent queries in fixed memory.
3. **Score** with time decay so last week counts more than last year (formula below).
4. **Filter**: remove queries on a blocklist (hate, violence, adult), and apply a **privacy threshold**: only consider queries searched by at least a minimum number of distinct users. This reduces rare-query exposure but does not guarantee privacy: sensitive information can be searched by many people or bots. Add explicit sensitive-data filtering and review.
5. **Build** the trie with top-k at every node (Spark job: for every query, emit `(prefix, query, score)` for each of its prefixes, group by prefix, keep the top k). With 100M queries and up to 20 prefixes each, that's up to 2 billion records to shuffle, a substantial batch workload whose duration depends on cluster resources.
6. **Publish** the serialised trie to object storage with a version number. Serving nodes download it, load it into memory alongside the current one, then publish the new root atomically with suitable synchronization. Retain the old trie snapshot until all readers using it finish. Roll out to a few nodes first and compare metrics, just like a code deploy.

The time-decayed score in step 3 weights each day's searches by how old they are:

```formula
score = Σ(count_d × 0.9^{age_d})
0.9^{6.6} ≈ 0.5
0.9^{30} ≈ 0.04
where
score: the query's ranking score
Σ: sigma, "add up over every day d" in the history
d: one day of history
count_d: how many times the query was searched on day d
age_d: how many days ago day d was (0 for today)
0.9^{age_d}: age_d copies of 0.9 multiplied together, the weight for that day; it shrinks by 10% per day of age
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: each day of age multiplies a search's weight by 0.9, so a search's weight halves roughly every 6.6 days and a month-old search keeps only about 4%.
```

The decay factor sets the trade-off: closer to 1 (say 0.98) keeps long-term favourites; smaller (say 0.7) makes suggestions chase the last few days.

### Freshness for trending queries

A daily rebuild can't surface "earthquake in Tokyo" ten minutes after it happens. Add a small **trending overlay**: the stream aggregator tracks queries whose last-hour count is far above their baseline, and the suggest service merges this small "trending" list into results for matching prefixes. The big trie stays daily; only a few thousand trending entries change minute to minute.

### Removing a suggestion urgently

Sometimes a suggestion must disappear *now*: a defamatory phrase, a victim's name, a legal takedown. Waiting for tomorrow's build isn't acceptable, and the CDN may hold the bad response for its whole TTL. So:

- Keep a small **serve-time blocklist** that every suggest node checks before returning results. It's pushed in seconds, like a config change.
- **Purge** affected prefixes using the selected CDN's documented purge mechanism, or keep edge TTLs short enough that the worst-case exposure is acceptable.
- Add the term to the pipeline's blocklist so the next build drops it at source.

## Key takeaways

- Rank submitted searches with explicit decay and eligibility rules.
- A distinct-user threshold reduces rare exposure but is not a privacy guarantee.
- Combine a trending overlay, serve-time blocklist and cache purge for urgent changes.

## Further reading

- [Meta: the life of a typeahead query](https://engineering.fb.com/2010/05/17/web/the-life-of-a-typeahead-query/)
- [Exponential decay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exponential_decay)

questions.prompt: Your trie rebuilds once a day. Product wants breaking-news queries (e.g. a major earthquake) to appear in suggestions **within 10 minutes**. What's the most practical design?

options.text: Add a small trending overlay: a stream job detects queries spiking above their baseline and publishes a small trending list that the suggest service merges into results.
options.explanation: Correct. Bound the trending layer to an explicit candidate budget and index by prefix. The main trie remains a daily artifact; measure merge latency and enforce the same safety/privacy filtering on both paths.

options.text: Update trie nodes in place on the serving nodes on every search.
options.explanation: Wrong. Updating top-k lists along every prefix path on every search means ~20 writes per search at 1B+ searches a day, with locking on hot nodes like 's'. It destroys the read-only simplicity that makes serving fast.

options.text: Rebuild the full trie every 10 minutes.
options.explanation: Wrong. A full rebuild aggregates weeks of logs and processes hundreds of millions of queries; meeting a ten-minute rebuild cadence requires resources and measured completion time that this design has not established, and each rebuild plus rollout might not even finish in 10 minutes.

options.text: Lower the CDN TTL to zero.
options.explanation: Wrong. Edge caching isn't the bottleneck; even with no caching, the underlying trie wouldn't contain the new query until the next daily build.

questions.workedExample:
This is the lambda-architecture pattern: a large, slow, accurate batch view plus a small, fast speed layer.

1. Stream job (Flink) counts queries in 1-minute tumbling windows.
2. Flag a query as trending when its recent count far exceeds its usual level, and distinct users exceed a threshold (to resist manipulation):

```formula
c_10 > 20 × base
where
c_10: searches for the query in the last 10 minutes
base: its usual (baseline) count for a 10-minute period
>: is greater than
In words: a query is trending when it is being searched more than 20 times as often as normal.
```

3. Publish the trending set (a few thousand entries) to the suggest service every minute.
4. At request time, take the trie's top-10 for the prefix, merge any trending queries matching that prefix with a boosted score, and return the top 10.

Keep an explicit candidate budget and a prefix index; benchmark merging and filter checks against the serving latency target. A small overlay does not by itself prove negligible latency.

questions.prompt: A privacy review finds that a user's unusual search, including their full home address, appeared as a suggestion for others. Which pipeline change reduces this class of exposure while acknowledging that popularity alone cannot prove privacy?

options.text: Add the user's address to the blocklist.
options.explanation: Wrong as a fix. It removes this one case but not the class of problem; every other user's private query can still leak. Blocklists are for known bad terms, not for unpredictable personal data.

options.text: Encrypt the search logs at rest.
options.explanation: Wrong. Encryption protects logs from unauthorised access, but the pipeline still decrypts and counts them. The query would still become a suggestion.

options.text: Shorten the CDN TTL so the suggestion disappears faster.
options.explanation: Wrong. This only changes how long cached copies live; the next trie build would still include the query.

options.text: Require a distinct-user eligibility threshold plus sensitive-data filtering and review; do not treat the threshold as a privacy guarantee.
options.explanation: Correct. A threshold suppresses rare queries, but addresses and other personal information can be searched by many people or attacker accounts. Approximate distinct counts can also overestimate; validate eligibility conservatively.

questions.workedExample:
Find where private data enters the suggestions: the aggregator counts raw searches, and a single user searching the same thing repeatedly can push it high enough for a narrow prefix.

Fix it at aggregation:

This Python fixture implements the distinct-identity threshold for one locale. Its input identities are assumed eligible; bot detection and sensitive-data filtering remain separate requirements.

```python
# Fixture: repeated events from one user
# still count as only one identity.
events = {
    "rare": ["u1"] * 100,
    "popular": [
        f"u{i}" for i in range(50)
    ],
}
keep = []
for query, users in events.items():
    # Count each eligible identity once.
    distinct_users = len(set(users))
    if distinct_users < 50:
        continue
    keep.append(query)
print(keep)
# ['popular']: rare has only one user.
```

A HyperLogLog can estimate candidate popularity, but its probabilistic estimate alone cannot prove that a strict eligibility threshold was reached. Counting distinct users also resists manipulation, since a bot repeating a phrase from one account gains nothing. Then add a blocklist and PII detectors (addresses, phone numbers) as additional risk reduction, with explicit review and removal procedures; none of these alone guarantees privacy.

questions.prompt:
Ranking uses a time-decayed score:

```formula
score = Σ(count_d × 0.9^{age_d})
where
score: a query's ranking score
Σ: sigma, "add up over every day d"
d: one day in the history being summed
count_d: searches for the query on day d
age_d: how many days ago day d was (0 for today)
0.9^{age_d}: age_d copies of 0.9 multiplied together
In words: every day of age multiplies a day's searches by 0.9.
```

Query A had **10,000** searches exactly **14 days ago** and none since. Query B has **2,000** searches **today** and none before. Which ranks higher today?

options.text: B, because recent searches always outrank older ones.
options.explanation: Wrong. Decay reduces old counts gradually; it doesn't zero them. Whether recent beats old depends on the numbers.

options.text: A, with a score of about 2,290 versus B's 2,000.
options.explanation: Correct. Fourteen days of the stated daily decay leave about 23%, so A keeps about 23% of its 10,000. That's still more than B's undecayed 2,000, under the given one-day histories. At age 16 days, A falls below a fixed 2,000-point benchmark. If both queries receive no new traffic, B also decays: their score ratio stays constant, so B does not overtake A merely as time passes.

options.text: A, with a score of 10,000, because decay only applies after 30 days.
options.explanation: Wrong. The formula decays every day's count by its age; nothing in it waits 30 days.
Wrong. The decay is exponential (0.9 raised to the 14th power), not multiplied by the age.

questions.workedExample:
Apply the decay factor. Squaring the 7-day factor gives the 14-day one:

```formula
0.9^7 ≈ 0.478
0.9^{14} = (0.9^7)^2 ≈ 0.229
A = 10,000 × 0.229 ≈ 2,290
B = 2,000 × 0.9^0 = 2,000 × 1 = 2,000
where
0.9^7: 7 copies of 0.9 multiplied together
0.9^0: anything to the power 0 is 1, so today's searches count in full
A, B: the two queries' scores today
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: after 14 days A keeps about 23% of its 10,000 searches, about 2,290, which still beats B's 2,000.
```

A factor of 0.9/day means a half-life (the time for a weight to halve) of about 6.6 days. If you want trending queries to win faster, lower the factor (e.g. 0.7/day gives a half-life of ~2 days) or add the trending overlay, which is designed for minutes-scale freshness.

questions.prompt: Legal asks you to remove a defamatory suggestion **immediately**. Suggestions are cached at the CDN for 10 minutes and the trie rebuilds nightly. Which steps belong in your answer? Select all that apply.

options.text: Push the phrase to a serve-time blocklist that every suggest node checks before responding.
options.explanation: Correct. A small blocklist distributed like config takes effect in seconds on the origin, without waiting for a rebuild.

options.text: Purge the affected prefixes from the CDN.
options.explanation: Correct. Otherwise the edge keeps serving the cached response for up to 10 minutes after the origin is fixed.

options.text: Add the phrase to the pipeline's blocklist so tonight's build drops it at source.
options.explanation: Correct. The serve-time list is a stopgap; fixing the source stops it reappearing in the next snapshot.

options.text: Trigger an immediate full rebuild and wait for it to roll out.
options.explanation: Incorrect as the main action. No rebuild duration is established here, and rebuilding still leaves existing CDN copies stale. It's far slower than the blocklist plus purge.

options.text: Set the CDN TTL to zero permanently.
options.explanation: Incorrect. It sacrifices most of your offload to handle a rare event that purging handles well.

questions.workedExample:
Trace every layer where the bad suggestion lives:

| Layer | Lifetime | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Trie snapshot | until rebuild | pipeline blocklist |
| Suggest node | until rebuild | serve-time blocklist |
| CDN | 10 min | purge |
| Browser | its cache TTL | accept, or keep short |

A strong answer names each layer and the fastest lever for it.

questions.prompt: Bots search "cheap pills brand-x" 500,000 times in a day from 300 accounts so it becomes a top suggestion for "cheap". Your pipeline already has a 50-distinct-user threshold. What's the best additional defence?

options.text: Rank by distinct users (or cap each user's contribution), and flag queries whose growth is concentrated in a few accounts or IPs.
options.explanation: Correct. 300 accounts doing 500k searches is ~1,700 each, nothing like organic behaviour. Counting each user at most a few times strips most of the inflated count, and concentration anomalies flag the campaign.

options.text: Raise the distinct-user threshold to 1,000.
options.explanation: Partly helps, but attackers can create more accounts, and a high threshold hides genuine niche queries for smaller locales. It's a blunt tool on its own.

options.text: Sample logs 1 in 100 so the bot's searches mostly get dropped.
options.explanation: Wrong. Uniform independent sampling reduces bot and human counts in the same proportion in expectation. Random variation can change ranks, but it does not selectively remove the manipulation.

options.text: Turn off suggestions for the prefix "cheap".
options.explanation: Wrong. It removes a useful prefix for everyone and the bots simply move to another prefix.

questions.workedExample:
Compare organic and bot patterns:

```formula
a = 500,000 / 300 ≈ 1,700
capped = 300 × 3 = 900
where
a: searches per bot account in a day
capped: the query's count if each user can contribute at most 3 per day
≈: approximately equal to (rounded from 1,667)
In words: each bot account searched about 1,700 times; capping every user at 3 cuts the bot query's count to 900.
```

With that cap the bot query's count falls to ~900, far below genuinely popular queries. Add anomaly detection on concentration (share of volume from the top 1% of users or IPs) to catch it outright.

lessons.title: Scale shared candidates across locales and users
lessons.summary: Benchmark core capacity at the target latency before sizing.
lessons.body:
## Deep dive 2: Scaling the serving path

If a representative benchmark establishes 1,000 requests/s per core at the target latency, the core count is the peak rate divided by that:

```formula
cores = peak / cap
cores = 180,000/s / (1,000/s) = 180
where
cores: CPU cores needed if every one runs flat out
peak: peak suggestion requests per second
cap: requests per second one core handles, an assumed 1,000
/s: per second
In words: 180,000 requests a second at an assumed 1,000 per core needs 180 fully busy cores, before headroom and before the CDN takes its share.
```

So 180,000/s requires 180 fully utilized cores before headroom and cache offload. A 1 ms response time alone does not establish CPU cost or throughput.

> [!note] Content gap: index and serving benchmarks
> No reproducible 100-million-query corpus, memory layout or serving benchmark is supplied. The 30–50 GB index size and per-core throughput are hypothetical sizing inputs, not guarantees.

### Edge and browser caching

Suggestions for a given prefix are the **same for everyone** in a locale (until personalisation). That makes them perfectly cacheable:

- Short prefixes are both the most requested (every query starts with one or two characters) and the most cacheable. The number of possible short prefixes depends on the alphabet and Unicode normalization; it is not necessarily a few thousand for every locale.
- A CDN with a 5–15 minute TTL can serve a large fraction of all requests without ever reaching your servers.
- The browser caches responses too, so backspacing costs nothing.

### Sharding, if it outgrows one machine

Suppose many locales and personal history push the index past what one machine holds.

- **Shard by locale** first: natural, and requests never cross locales.
- **Shard by prefix range** (a–f, g–m...) is tempting but **skewed**: far more English queries start with "s" or "c" than "x" or "q". Use ranges sized by measured traffic, or shard by hash of the first few characters.
- With a flattened `prefix → list` KV store, hashing spreads distinct prefixes, but a very hot prefix still maps to one shard and may need replicas or caching.

## Deep dive 3: Ranking and personalisation

Popularity alone is a decent baseline. Real systems use a **two-stage** approach:

1. **Candidate generation**: the trie returns the top ~50 by global score. Fast and cacheable.
2. **Re-ranking**: a lightweight model reorders the candidates using context: the user's location, language, recent searches, time of day.

Personalisation prevents sharing the same final cached response across users unless the cache key safely separates their results. A common compromise: cache the global top-50 at the edge, and do the personal re-ranking (or blend in the user's own recent searches) on the client or in a thin per-user service.

Facebook's original typeahead took personalisation further: when you focused the search box, it preloaded your friends and frequently visited pages into the browser, so the first few characters were matched entirely client-side.

## Key takeaways

- Benchmark core capacity at the target latency before sizing.
- Cache shared locale-specific candidates and personalise after that stage.
- Partition by measured traffic and protect very hot prefixes with replicas or caching.

## Further reading

- [Meta: the life of a typeahead query](https://engineering.fb.com/2010/05/17/web/the-life-of-a-typeahead-query/)
- [Elasticsearch: completion suggesters](https://www.elastic.co/docs/reference/elasticsearch/rest-apis/search-suggesters)
- [RFC 9111: HTTP caching](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9111.html)

questions.prompt: You add personalised re-ranking based on each user's recent searches. Your CDN previously served 60% of suggestion traffic. What's the best way to keep most of that offload?

options.text: Include the user ID in the cache key so each user's results are cached at the edge.
options.explanation: Wrong. Per-user cache keys destroy hit rates: each user's prefixes are requested only a few times, so almost every request misses and goes to the origin.

options.text: Disable the CDN; personalisation requires every request to reach the origin.
options.explanation: Wrong. It would roughly 2.5x the origin's load (from 40% to 100% of traffic). Personalisation doesn't require giving up shared caching if you split the work.

options.text: Keep caching the global top-N per prefix at the edge, and apply personal re-ranking or blending on the client (or a thin per-user service) on top of those candidates.
options.explanation: Correct. The expensive, shared part (candidate generation) stays cacheable. The personal part is small: re-order 50 candidates and mix in a handful of the user's recent queries, which the client already knows.

options.text: Precompute a personalised trie per user.
options.explanation: Wrong. With hundreds of millions of users, a 40 GB trie per user is absurd. Even small per-user tries would be a massive storage and rebuild cost for little benefit.

questions.workedExample:
Split the response into **shared** and **personal** parts:

| Part | Varies by | Cacheable at edge? |
|---|---|---|
| Global top-50 for prefix | prefix, locale | Yes |
| Recent searches, re-rank | user | Not shared across users |

The client fetches the global list (CDN hit), then merges in the user's recent searches it stores locally and applies a lightweight re-ranker. The origin still sees ~40% of traffic, as before. This is the general pattern: cache what's common, compute what's personal as late and as close to the user as possible.

questions.prompt: With 50 locales and personal history, the index grows to **400 GB**, too big for one machine. English is 40% of traffic. What sharding scheme is most sensible?

options.text: Shard by locale first; split large locales like English further by a hash of the prefix (or traffic-sized prefix ranges), and replicate each shard.
options.explanation: Correct. Locale is a natural boundary (no request crosses it). Hashing spreads distinct prefixes but cannot split one hot prefix; use caching/replication for that key, and replicas give throughput and redundancy.

options.text: Shard by first letter across 26 machines for all locales together.
options.explanation: Wrong. Letter distribution is heavily skewed (many more queries begin with 's' than 'x'), and non-Latin scripts don't map onto 26 letters at all.

options.text: Shard by user ID so personal history stays together.
options.explanation: Wrong. Most of the index is global, so every request would have to fan out to every shard to find completions for a prefix.

options.text: Store it in one 400 GB process with swap enabled.
options.explanation: Wrong. Paging trie nodes to disk turns microsecond lookups into millisecond ones and wrecks tail latency.

questions.workedExample:
Pick the shard key from the request: every request carries a locale and a prefix.

1. **Locale**: no cross-locale requests, so locale shards are independent.
2. **Within English** (the largest): hash the full prefix (with a flattened `prefix → list` store) or use ranges sized by measured traffic.
3. **Replicate** each shard for throughput.

Avoid raw alphabetical ranges: the busiest letters get many times the load of the quietest.

lessons.title: Roll out suggestion snapshots safely as traffic grows
lessons.summary: Validate sample lookups, size and filtering before publication.
lessons.body:
Serving nodes use immutable trie snapshots built offline. A bad snapshot can make suggestions empty or unsafe across an entire region, so a snapshot rollout deserves the same controlled deployment process as application code.

## Bottlenecks and trade-offs

| Decision | Trade-off |
|---|---|
| Top-k at each node | Fast reads, more RAM |
| Daily rebuild | Simple, stale |
| Trending overlay | Fresh, more moving parts |
| Edge caching | Huge offload, no personalisation |

Failure modes to mention:

- **Bad trie snapshot**: a pipeline bug ships an empty or offensive trie. Validate trie snapshots (size, sample lookups, blocklist check) before publishing, and keep the previous version for instant rollback.
- **Manipulation**: bots search a phrase repeatedly to make it a suggestion. Count distinct users rather than raw searches and apply anomaly detection.
- **Slow responses are worse than none**: if the service doesn't answer within ~50 ms, the client should give up; a late suggestion for an old prefix is just noise.

## At 10x scale

At 10 billion searches/day with 50 locales:

```formula
peak = 10B × 6 / (10^5 s) × 3 ≈ 1.8M/s
where
peak: peak suggestion requests per second
B: billion
M: million
6: suggestion requests per search
10^5: 100,000, the seconds in a day rounded
3: the assumed peak factor
s: seconds; /s means per second
≈: approximately equal to
In words: ten times the searches gives about 1.8 million, call it 2 million, suggestion requests a second at peak.
```

That is about 2M suggestion requests/s at peak. Then:

- **Edge first**: push the most popular prefixes' responses into CDN workers' memory; the origin sees only the long tail.
- **Partition by locale and region**, each with its own trie and its own replicas.
- **Rebuild incrementally**: instead of recomputing everything daily, apply hourly deltas for queries whose scores changed significantly.
- **Richer ranking** through the two-stage model, with the re-ranker deployed close to users.
- **Fuzzy matching** (typos) via Levenshtein automata over the FST, which Lucene supports, at the cost of more CPU per lookup.

## A safe snapshot handover

Build and validate a versioned artifact before announcing it as current. A canary downloads it, checks integrity and performs representative lookups, including blocked terms and locales. It loads the new trie alongside the old trie, then changes the root with appropriate synchronisation. Readers that started on the old root must be allowed to finish before that memory is released.

Compare error rates, latency, result coverage and suspicious changes against the previous version. Roll out gradually across regions and retain the old artifact so rollback changes a version pointer rather than waiting for a rebuild. A root swap prevents readers seeing a partly built structure; it does not prove that the contents are correct. Validation, canaries and rollback address that separate risk.

## Key takeaways

- Validate sample lookups, size and filtering before publication.
- Canary snapshots and retain a usable rollback version.
- Use edge serving, locale partitions and incremental updates as measured pressure grows.

## Further reading

- [Finite-state transducers and compact indexes](https://burntsushi.net/transducers/)
- [Elasticsearch: completion suggesters](https://www.elastic.co/docs/reference/elasticsearch/rest-apis/search-suggesters)

questions.prompt: A new nightly trie snapshot is ready. Which practices make the swap safe on serving nodes? Select all that apply.

options.text: Load the new trie snapshot alongside the old one and swap a pointer atomically, so requests never see a half-loaded trie.
options.explanation: Correct. Readers keep using the old version until the new one is fully built in memory; the root publication must use synchronization appropriate to the runtime, and old trie snapshots must remain alive for existing readers.

options.text: Provision RAM for two trie snapshots, since both are resident during the swap.
options.explanation: Correct. A 50 GB index needs ~100 GB during the swap. Forgetting this leads to out-of-memory kills exactly at deploy time.

options.text: Validate the trie snapshot (size, sample lookups, blocklist check) and roll it to a few canary nodes first.
options.explanation: Correct. A pipeline bug can produce an empty or offensive trie. Validation and a canary stop it reaching everyone.

options.text: Delete the previous trie snapshot from object storage as soon as the new one is published.
options.explanation: Incorrect. Keeping the previous version allows instant rollback if the canary or metrics look wrong.

options.text: Restart all serving nodes at once so they pick up the new file together.
options.explanation: Incorrect. A simultaneous restart drops capacity to zero and a bad trie snapshot would hit every user at once.

questions.workedExample:
Treat a trie snapshot like a code deploy:

```
1. build -> validate -> publish v42
2. canary: 2 nodes load v42
3. compare metrics vs v41
4. roll out region by region
5. keep v41 for rollback
```

In memory, each node does: load v42 → build structures → synchronized root swap → wait for old readers → free v41. Peak RAM is both versions at once.

lessons.title: Estimate notification volume, burst and channel cost
lessons.summary: Separate channel mix from total volume and campaign bursts.
lessons.body:
Almost every product sends notifications: password reset codes, "your order has shipped", "Sam liked your photo", weekly digests, marketing campaigns. Rather than every team integrating with Apple, Google, Twilio and an email provider separately, companies build one notification platform that every service calls.

The interesting problems aren't sending a message, which is one API call to a provider. They are: never letting a marketing blast delay a login code, minimising duplicate alerts, respecting what users have opted out of, and coping when a provider has an outage.

## Step 1: Requirements

**Functional**

- Internal services send notifications to users via **push** (iOS, Android), **SMS**, **email** and **in-app**.
- Messages are built from **notification templates** with parameters and language localisation (`order_shipped`, `en-GB`).
- **User preferences**: opt in/out per category (security, social, marketing) and per channel; quiet hours in the user's time zone.
- **Scheduling**: send now, or at a given time (including "9 am local time" for each recipient).
- **Bulk campaigns**: send to an audience segment of millions of users.
- **Tracking**: sent, delivered, opened, failed.

**Non-functional**

- **Priority-aware latency**: a one-time passcode (OTP) within a few seconds; social notifications within a minute; marketing within hours is fine.
- **Reliable**: durable retries within a bounded TTL and attempt budget, with deduplication to reduce repeats. Neither delivery nor duplicate-free presentation is guaranteed.
- **Scalable** to billions per day, with large bursts from campaigns.
- **Resilient** to provider outages and rate limits.
- **Compliant**: unsubscribe must work; marketing consent rules (GDPR, PECR in the UK, TCPA in the US) must be honoured.

## Step 2: Estimates

Assume **200 million daily active users** and on average **5 notifications per user per day**.

```formula
total = 200M × 5 = 1B/day
avg = 1B / (10^5 s) ≈ 10,000/s
where
total: notifications per day
avg: average notifications per second
M: million (10^6)
B: billion (10^9)
day: one day; /day means per day
10^5: 100,000, the seconds in a day (86,400) rounded up
s: seconds; /s means per second
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: 200 million users receiving 5 notifications a day is a billion a day, about 10,000 a second on average.
```

Channel mix, say 85% push, 12% email, 3% SMS. Each channel's rate is its share of the total:

```formula
push = 0.85 × 10,000/s = 8,500/s
email = 0.12 × 10,000/s = 1,200/s
sms = 0.03 × 10,000/s = 300/s
where
push, email, sms: average sends per second on each channel (850 million, 120 million and 30 million a day)
0.85, 0.12, 0.03: each channel's share of all notifications (85%, 12%, 3%)
/s: per second
In words: most of the volume is push; SMS is only 300 a second, but it is the expensive one.
```

Campaigns create bursts on top. Sending to 50M users within an hour adds:

```formula
burst = 50,000,000 / (3,600 s) ≈ 14,000/s
peak = 3 × 10,000/s = 30,000/s
where
burst: extra sends per second from one campaign spread over an hour
3,600 s: the seconds in one hour
peak: the normal daily peak, three times the average
s: seconds; /s means per second
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: one 50-million-user campaign over an hour adds about 14,000 a second on top of a normal peak of about 30,000 a second.
```

So design for **30–50k/s** peaks.

For an illustrative cost model, assume $0.01 per single-segment SMS, excluding other fees:

```formula
daily = 30M × $0.01 = $300,000
yearly = $300,000 × 365 = $109.5M
where
daily, yearly: SMS spend per day and per 365-day year
M: million
$: US dollars
In words: 30 million texts a day at a cent each costs $300,000 a day, about $110 million a year.
```

So 30M/day costs $300,000/day, or $109.5M per 365-day year. Actual rates depend on destination, provider, sender and segment count. Reducing unnecessary SMS and duplicates matters.

> **Content gap:** no current provider quote or production throughput benchmark is supplied. Rates and capacity here are scenario assumptions, not measured service characteristics.

Storage for the notification log at ~500 B (bytes) per record:

```formula
daily = 1 bn × 500 B = 500 GB
kept = 500 GB × 90 = 45 TB
where
daily: new log data per day
kept: data held with 90-day retention (records older than 90 days deleted)
bn: billion (10^9) records per day
B: bytes
GB: gigabyte, 10^9 bytes
TB: terabyte, 10^12 bytes (1,000 GB)
In words: a billion 500-byte records a day is 500 GB a day, and keeping 90 days of them takes 45 TB.
```

## Key takeaways

- Separate channel mix from total volume and campaign bursts.
- Use an explicitly hypothetical per-segment SMS rate.
- Include log retention and duplicate reduction in the capacity and cost model.

## Further reading

- [Twilio: SMS encoding and segment limits](https://www.twilio.com/docs/glossary/what-sms-character-limit)
- [Azure: priority queue pattern](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/patterns/priority-queue)

questions.prompt: You send **1.2 billion** notifications/day: 85% push, 12% email, 3% SMS. Assume a hypothetical **$0.01 per single-segment SMS**, excluding additional fees. What is the approximate daily SMS cost, and what does it suggest?

options.text: About $3,600/day; SMS cost is negligible.
options.explanation: Wrong. This is 100x too low; it treats 3% as 0.03% (360,000 messages). The real volume is 36 million.

options.text: About $360,000/day; it's worth using push first and falling back to SMS only when push isn't delivered or opened.
options.explanation: Correct. 1.2B × 3% = 36M SMS; × $0.01 = $360,000/day, over $130M a year. Push-first escalation and strict dedup on SMS save real money.

options.text: About $12M/day; SMS should be removed entirely.
options.explanation: Wrong. That's the cost if *every* notification were an SMS. And removing SMS entirely would break OTPs for users without the app installed.

options.text: About $36,000/day; switch everything to SMS for reliability.
options.explanation: Wrong. The arithmetic is 10x too low, and moving everything to SMS would multiply costs about 33x for little gain.

questions.workedExample:
```formula
sms = 1.2B × 0.03 = 36M/day
daily = 36M × $0.01 = $360,000
yearly = $360,000 × 365 ≈ $131M
where
sms: SMS messages per day, 3% (0.03) of all notifications
daily, yearly: SMS spend per day and per year
B: billion
M: million
day: one day; /day means per day
$: US dollars
≈: approximately equal to (rounded)
In words: 3% of 1.2 billion is 36 million texts a day; at a cent each that is $360,000 a day, about $131 million a year.
```

Implications you'd say out loud:

- **Channel escalation**: send push; if not opened within 5 minutes, send SMS. Even converting a third of SMS to push saves ~$40M a year.
- **Dedup matters financially**: a 1% duplicate rate on SMS is ~$1.3M a year.
- **Clean phone numbers**: invalid numbers cost money and hurt sender reputation.

lessons.title: Accept recoverable work into an asynchronous pipeline
lessons.summary: 202 means accepted work rather than confirmed delivery.
lessons.body:
The sizing scenario reaches billions of notifications a day across push, SMS, email and in-app channels. This unit connects the producer contract to recoverable queued work, preferences and delivery records.

## Step 3: API

```
POST /v1/notifications
{
  "idempotencyKey": "order-8812-shipped",
  "userId": "u_123",
  "template": "order_shipped",
  "params": {"orderId": "8812"},
  "category": "transactional",
  "priority": "high",
  "channels": ["push", "email"],
  "sendAt": null,
  "ttlSeconds": 86400
}
-> 202 Accepted {notificationId}
```

Notes:

- **202 Accepted** explicitly represents work accepted for asynchronous processing. A 200 response can also describe a successful enqueue operation under another API contract; it does not inherently mean delivered.
- `idempotencyKey` is required. The order service might retry; the same key must not produce a second notification.
- `ttlSeconds` says when the notification becomes pointless. Stop initiating retries at expiry, request provider-side expiry where supported, and enforce OTP validity on the server: an already queued SMS may still arrive late.
- Campaigns use a separate endpoint that takes an **audience segment** and a schedule, rather than millions of individual calls.

## Step 4: Data model

```
devices
  user_id, device_id (PK)
  platform (ios|android|web)
  push_token, app_version
  last_seen

preferences
  user_id, category, channel (PK)
  enabled, updated_at
  + timezone, quiet_hours per user

templates
  name, channel, locale, version (PK)
  subject, body (with placeholders)

notifications (log)
  user_id, created_at, notification_id (PK)
  idempotency_key, template, channel
  status, attempts, provider_msg_id
  created_at, sent_at, delivered_at
```

Devices and preferences are read on every send, so cache them (Redis, or in-memory in workers) keyed by `user_id`. The notification log is write-heavy and queried by `user_id` and time ("what did we send this user?"), which suits Cassandra or DynamoDB partitioned by `user_id` with a time-ordered sort key.

## Step 5: High-level design

```
 Producers (auth, orders,
 social, campaign scheduler)
          |
          v
 Notification API
 (validate, idempotency)
          |
          v
 Kafka: critical | high | low
          |
          v
 Processor workers
 (prefs, caps, template)
          |
   +------+------+------+
   v      v      v      v
  push   sms   email  in-app
 queue  queue  queue  queue
   |      |      |      |
   v      v      v      v
 APNs/  Twilio/ SES/  websocket
 FCM    Vonage  SendGrid / inbox
```

1. The **API** validates the request, atomically claims the idempotency key and writes an `accepted` record plus an outbox event; a relay publishes that event to the priority topic.
2. **Processor workers** load the user's preferences and devices, drop channels the user has opted out of, apply frequency caps and quiet hours, render the template for each channel and locale, and enqueue one message per channel.
3. **Channel senders** call the providers, record the result, and handle retries.
4. **Webhooks** from providers (delivery receipts, bounces, unsubscribes) flow back into the log and the preferences store.

Each stage is separately scalable, and a slow email provider primarily backs up its own queue. Shared databases, networks and quotas also need isolation.

## Key takeaways

- 202 means accepted work rather than confirmed delivery.
- Claim idempotency with the accepted record and outbox in one durable transaction.
- Keep channel senders and provider callbacks as separately recoverable stages.

## Further reading

- [AWS: transactional outbox pattern](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/cloud-design-patterns/transactional-outbox.html)
- [RFC 9110: 202 Accepted](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-15.3.3)

questions.prompt: Why is **202 Accepted** a suitable response when this API accepts a notification for asynchronous processing?

options.text: Because the notification has only been queued; delivery happens asynchronously and may still fail or be suppressed by preferences.
options.explanation: 202 explicitly means accepted for processing, not completed. A different API may use 200 for a completed enqueue operation; 200 alone does not imply delivery.

options.text: Because 202 is faster for the client to parse.
options.explanation: Wrong. Status codes cost the same to parse. The choice is about meaning, not performance.

options.text: Because 200 is reserved for GET requests.
options.explanation: Wrong. 200 is valid for POST responses. The distinction is whether the action has completed, not the HTTP method.

options.text: Because 202 makes the client retry automatically.
options.explanation: Wrong. 202 doesn't trigger retries. Clients retry on timeouts and 5xx/429 errors; that's why the API also needs an idempotency key.

questions.workedExample:
Trace what happens after the API call:

1. API validates and writes a log row: `accepted`.
2. Message goes onto a Kafka topic.
3. A worker checks preferences: the user may have opted out, so it's *suppressed*.
4. A sender calls APNs, which may fail and be retried.

At the moment the API responds, only step 1 has happened. 202 plus a `notificationId` the caller can use to query status is the honest contract for asynchronous work.
